docs.title: Your first event
docs.text: Before a campaign, run one event through the whole chain and look at what comes out. This page does that twice: first one O+O event at 200 GeV with the Pythonic example oo_workflow.py (3D MC-Glauber, Pythia with initial-state radiation, MUSIC on the GPU, Matter + LBT, iColored and iSS: under a minute), then two Au+Au jet events with the production driver of the two-stage production. You need the production container, the xscape wheel on a Mac, or a source build.

docs.title: 1. One O+O event
docs.text:
oo_workflow.py reads a user XML (default: oo_workflow.xml next to it, made from the O+O production's template), runs the events and writes the bulk and jet hadrons of each event to two hadron files. The examples can't run inside the read-only image or the installed wheel (they write next to themselves), so xscape-examples first copies them into a directory of yours.

DockerApptainerMacSource build 
mkdir -p work
docker run --rm --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/work:/work" -w /work \
  jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 bash -c \
  'xscape-examples /work/examples && cd /work/examples/pythonic &&
   python oo_workflow.py --events 1 --outdir /work/out_oo'

The hadron files land in ./work/out_oo/. --gpus all gives the container the GPU and --user makes the files yours. Other CUDA versions (cu130 for Blackwell and GH200, cu124 for older drivers): Production container.

apptainer pull xscape_prod.sif docker://jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126
W=$SCRATCH/xscape; mkdir -p $W
apptainer exec --bind $W:/work xscape_prod.sif xscape-examples /work/examples
apptainer exec --nv --pwd /work/examples/pythonic --bind $W:/work xscape_prod.sif \
  python oo_workflow.py --events 1 --outdir /work/out_oo

Apptainer needs --nv for the GPU and --pwd for the working directory: it ignores the image's own and starts where you launched it. On a cluster run this on a GPU node (in a batch script, or after salloc).

source ~/.venvs/xscape-0.2.0/bin/activate      # the environment of the installation
xscape-examples ~/xscape/examples
cd ~/xscape/examples/pythonic
python oo_workflow.py --events 1 --outdir ~/xscape/out_oo

MUSIC runs on the Mac's GPU (Metal) without any setting; the event takes under a minute (27 s on an M3 Max). The LBT tables must have been fetched once (xscape-fetch-data lbt, part of the installation).

cd X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/pythonic
python oo_workflow.py --events 1 --outdir out_oo

In the environment PyJetscape was built in, with the jetscape package importable (Source build). The script finds the X-SCAPE tree it sits in and runs the build X-SCAPE/build_gpu, or the one $JETSCAPE_BUILD names (--build DIR overrides both).

The options of oo_workflow.py:

option default --xml FILE oo_workflow.xml the user XML: O+O 200 GeV, b < 3 fm, pT̂ 20–40 GeV, 20 iSS oversamples per event --events N the XML's (3) events --seed S the XML's (7) the framework seed --outdir DIR ./out_oo output directory --name NAME the XML's file name (oo_workflow) the file stem --build DIR $JETSCAPE_BUILD, else $XSCAPE/build_gpu the X-SCAPE build (leave it alone in the container and the wheel) --keep-workdir off keep the job's working directory OUTDIR/work/<name> with the modules' side files

docs.title: What it prints and writes
docs.text:
Between the modules' own log lines (MUSIC, iSS, LBT, Matter), the script prints one line per event and a summary. One event on an M3 Max (source build) gave:

oo_workflow: /…/out_oo/oo_workflow.xml
event 0: 17 final partons, 157350 surface cells, 8361 bulk hadrons, 116 jet hadrons, 15.7 s
oo_workflow: 1 event(s) written, skipped none
  /…/out_oo/oo_workflow_hadrons_jet_frag.h5
  /…/out_oo/oo_workflow_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5

The bulk-hadron count is summed over the event's 20 oversamples. In out_oo/:

file content oo_workflow.xml the job's XML as run, with --events and --seed applied oo_workflow_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5 the bulk: iSS on MUSIC's freeze-out surface, one sample per oversample, with the event record (pT̂, the Glauber numbers, seeds) per unit oo_workflow_hadrons_jet_frag.h5 the jet hadrons of iColoredHadronization, one sample per event, with the partons that started the showers (initiators/)

A module that throws inside an event costs that event only: it is listed as skipped, and the run goes on.

docs.title: A look at the hadrons
docs.text:
The files are in the jetscape.hadrons_h5 format of all productions. In the same environment (or the analysis environment, which needs no X-SCAPE):

import awkward as ak
import jetscape as js

jet = js.HadronArray.from_h5("out_oo/oo_workflow_hadrons_jet_frag.h5")
bulk = js.HadronArray.from_h5("out_oo/oo_workflow_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5")
print(jet, "|", bulk)          # HadronArray(116 hadrons in 1 samples) | HadronArray(8361 hadrons in 20 samples)
print(jet.info["units"]["pthat"])                 # the event record: pT-hat, Glauber numbers, seeds

b = bulk.to_awkward(by_unit=True)                 # events x oversamples x hadrons
ch = b[js.select(b, "charged")]
print(ak.mean(ak.num(ch[abs(ch.eta) < 0.5], axis=2)))   # dN_ch/deta at |eta| < 0.5, averaged over oversamples

The oversamples of one event share one fluid: average over them, they are not independent collisions. The notebook version of the run, pythonic/oo_workflow.ipynb, goes on from here: awkward views, PDG selections, spectra with errors, FastJet on every event and every oversample in one call. The interface is described in The Pythonic interface; the O+O analysis in O+O.

Make it yours

oo_workflow.py is also a template: change the XML (--xml my_job.xml) and the per-event block that decides what is stored. For a production with campaigns, seeds and restarts, use the O+O production itself: O+O with ISR.

docs.title: The same XML without Python: xscape-run
docs.text:
The user XML runs with X-SCAPE's own executable too, without the Python layer: then X-SCAPE's writers decide what is stored (here none are on, so set e.g. <JetScapeWriterFinalStateHadronsAscii> on </JetScapeWriterFinalStateHadronsAscii> in a copy). On a Mac:

xscape-run -w ~/xscape/runs/oo -u ~/xscape/examples/pythonic/oo_workflow.xml

xscape-run copies both XMLs into the run directory with their ../ paths made absolute (your file is not changed), links the tables, and checks the XML before it starts: tags the main XML lacks, inputs that aren't there, modules the wheel doesn't have. Each stops it with the reason (exit code 3). Plain runJetscape in a directory of yours stops and points to xscape-run: 3dMCGlauber and MUSIC read their tables from the working directory. Details: Mac, One XML. In a source build the script behind it is X-SCAPE/examples/run_in_workdir.sh -d BUILD -w RUN_DIR -u USER_XML, with the tag and input checks (the module checks are the wheel's).

docs.title: 2. Two Au+Au jet events
docs.text:
Now the main production's driver, run_prod_jet.py: two 0–10 % Au+Au events at 200 GeV, each a background and a jet leg (two MUSIC runs), with the freeze-out surfaces and the partons stored for hadronization (--write-particlize both). Then stage 2 turns them into hadrons on the CPU.

DockerApptainerMacSource build 
IMG=jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126
mkdir -p prod
# stage 1 (Docker starts in prod_AuAu_0_10_jet)
docker run --rm --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/prod:/work" $IMG \
  python run_prod_jet.py --events 2 --seed 1 --write-particlize both --outdir /work/out
# stage 2: no GPU
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/prod:/work" $IMG \
  python run_hadronize.py /work/out -j 4 --oversample 500 --n-frag 50

EX=/opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example
W=$SCRATCH/xscape; mkdir -p $W
# stage 1
apptainer exec --nv --pwd $EX/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet --bind $W:/work xscape_prod.sif \
  python run_prod_jet.py --events 2 --seed 1 --write-particlize both --outdir /work/out
# stage 2: no GPU, no --nv
apptainer exec --pwd $EX/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet --bind $W:/work xscape_prod.sif \
  python run_hadronize.py /work/out -j 4 --oversample 500 --n-frag 50

cd ~/xscape/examples/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet
# stage 1: about 40 s on an M3 Max
python run_prod_jet.py --events 2 --seed 1 --write-particlize both --outdir ~/xscape/prod/out
# stage 2, on the CPU
python run_hadronize.py ~/xscape/prod/out -j 4 --oversample 500 --n-frag 50

cd X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet
python run_prod_jet.py --events 2 --seed 1 --write-particlize both --outdir out
python run_hadronize.py out -j 4 --oversample 500 --n-frag 50

Put the output one level inside your directory

Every job records its seed in seeds_used.tsv in the parent of its output directory. So write to /work/out (or ~/xscape/prod/out), not to /work itself, whose parent is inside the read-only image.

With an explicit --seed 1 the stem is AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001. Stage 1 writes AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001.h5 (the hydro pair: the jet leg arr and the background arr_bg), AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001_particlize.h5 (both freeze-out surfaces and the final partons), the job's .xml and .json. Stage 2 writes next to the particlize file:

file hadrons <stem>_hadrons_bulk_jet.h5 iSS on the jet leg's surface: the bulk with the jet's wake <stem>_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5 iSS on the background's surface <stem>_hadrons_jet_frag.h5 the jet partons, fragmented by Pythia

The difference between the first two is the medium's response to the jet, at hadron level. Read the three together with HadronFileReader: Hadrons.

A first look at the hydro pair

arr - arr_bg is the jet's effect on the medium and nothing else: both legs start from the same initial condition and are bit-identical until the first droplet deposits. With h5py: f["arr"][0] - f["arr_bg"][0] for event 0 (channels energy density, vx, vy, vz). More in Hydro and hadrons together.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Au+Au jets (two stages): from these two events to a campaign.
  • O+O with ISR: the O+O production behind oo_workflow.py.
  • Notebooks: the analysis notebooks to run on these files.

docs.title: O+O with initial-state radiation
docs.text: prod_OO_isr runs O+O collisions at 200 GeV with X-SCAPE's initial-state radiation (ISR) workflow: the hard scattering's incoming partons are showered backward in time by iMATTER, the 3D MC-Glauber strings are made from what the hard scattering left, MUSIC evolves that medium, and Matter + LBT shower the jets through it. The jet hadrons come from iColoredHadronization, which follows the colour flow of the ISR and the beam remnants; the bulk hadrons from iSS. Use it for small-system studies where the hard process and the bulk come from the same nucleon–nucleon collisions: multiplicity and centrality biases of hard-triggered events, flow, jets in a small medium. The tuned O+O 3D MC-Glauber and MUSIC parameters are those of X-SCAPE's O+O example, tuned at 200 GeV.

docs.title: What is different from Au+Au
docs.text:
IS: 3dMCGlauber (O16, positions only)
 -> Hard: PythiaIsrGun at one binary collision
          -> IsrManager / iMATTER       ISR, backward in time
          -> MCGlauberGenString         strings, the hard partons' momentum subtracted
 -> MUSIC                              ONE hydro run per event
 -> Eloss: Matter + LBT in the medium   the final-state shower
 -> JetHadronization: iColored          jet hadrons, in the job
 -> SoftParticlization: iSS             bulk hadrons, in the job or later
  • One MUSIC run per event, no pair. The medium is made from what each event's hard scattering left (its partons' momentum is subtracted from the colliding nucleons), so a medium belongs to one hard event: there is no background leg, no jet − background, no hydro reuse, and no jet deposition into the fluid.
  • Every event is hard-triggered: exactly one hard scattering, at a binary collision drawn uniformly. glauber_ncoll is recorded per event to weight the geometry (O+O analysis). Centrality comes from the impact parameter: the default b < 3 fm is about 0–24 % of the O+O cross section.
  • The jet hadrons are made in the job. iColoredHadronization needs the event's beam remnants and ISR colour connections, which exist only while the job runs. The bulk can be made in the job or later from stored surfaces.
  • Events without a medium: when the hard collision is the only one, no string is made; Matter showers in vacuum and the bulk unit is empty (has_medium 0).
  • The cores set the rate. An O+O event is small (MUSIC's grid ±10.5 fm), so an O+O job needs ~1.4 GB and ~6 core-s per event; the GPU is far from full.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
The driver is run_prod_oo_isr.py (one job), with the same run_jobs.sh as the Au+Au productions: the same seeds, campaign names, seed registry and restarts (Au+Au jets).

python run_prod_oo_isr.py --events 1 --seed 1 --dry-run      # check the XML/grid, print the plan
python run_prod_oo_isr.py --events 10 --seed 1               # pT-hat 20-40 GeV, b < 3 fm
python run_prod_oo_isr.py --events 30 --seed 1 --pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-40 --parton-ymax 0.6
./run_jobs.sh 20 25 0                                        # 20 jobs x 25 events, unique seeds
./run_jobs.sh -j 2 20 25 1 out_had --bulk-hadrons 100 --no-particlize

The image starts in the Au+Au folder, so point it at the O+O one, or call the scripts by their full path (they find their XML and grid next to themselves):

DockerApptainerMac 
OO=/opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_OO_isr
docker run --rm --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -e OMP_NUM_THREADS=3 -e OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive -e MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC=block \
  -v "$HOME/prod:/work" -w "$OO" jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 \
  ./run_jobs.sh -j 8 --mps 32 60 0 /work/OO_a --bulk-hadrons 100 --no-particlize --no-hydro-file

OO=/opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_OO_isr
apptainer exec --nv --env OMP_NUM_THREADS=3,OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive,MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC=block \
  --pwd "$OO" --bind "$SCRATCH/prod:/work" xscape_prod.sif \
  ./run_jobs.sh -j 8 32 60 0 /work/OO_a --bulk-hadrons 100 --no-particlize --no-hydro-file

cd ~/xscape/examples/prod_OO_isr
python run_prod_oo_isr.py --events 2 --seed 5 --outdir ~/xscape/prod/out_oo
OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive KMP_BLOCKTIME=0 \
  ./run_jobs.sh -j 3 --campaign oo_a 20 25 0 ~/xscape/prod/OO_a --bulk-hadrons 100 --no-particlize

That is 32 jobs × 60 events, 8 at a time on one GPU, with all hadrons made in the jobs and nothing else kept. Write the output under the bound /work: the default ./out is inside the read-only image. Nothing needs to be set for iMATTER in the container (the image sets PYTHIA8DATA), and the LBT table cache and --stagger don't apply to these small jobs.

docs.title: Hadronization: in the job or afterwards
docs.text:
setup options files afterwards A. everything in the job --bulk-hadrons 100 --no-particlize <stem>.h5, _hadrons_bulk_bg.h5, _hadrons_jet_frag.h5 nothing to do B. in the job, surfaces kept --bulk-hadrons 100 A + _particlize.h5 more oversamples or other iSS settings any time C. bulk afterwards (the default) none <stem>.h5, _particlize.h5, _hadrons_jet_frag.h5 hadronize.py --tags bulk_bg

Add --no-hydro-file to any of them to leave out the hydro evolution (MUSIC still runs and Matter still reads it). A + --no-hydro-file is a hadrons-only job: the usual production setting, at ~0.13 MB per event with 10 oversamples.

For setup C, the bulk is made on CPUs with the Au+Au production's hadronize.py, always with --tags bulk_bg (the jet hadrons were made in the job; it refuses jet_frag on these files):

python ../prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/hadronize.py out/OO_isr_seed0001_particlize.h5 \
       --tags bulk_bg --oversample 100
python ../prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/run_hadronize.py out -j 4 --tags bulk_bg --oversample 100

In the container, with -w "$OO" (Docker) or --pwd "$OO" (Apptainer) and without --gpus/--nv: ../prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/run_hadronize.py /work/OO_a -j 8 --tags bulk_bg --oversample 100. On SLURM: PROD=oo for utils/slurm_hadronize.sh (Clusters).

The bulk made in the job and afterwards are sampled alike (both use config/hadronize.xml); only the seeds differ. An event at hadron level is unit i of the jet file plus unit i of the bulk file; the bulk's N oversamples share one fluid.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
option default --pthat-min, --pthat-max 20, 40 GeV one pT̂ window --pthat-bins A-B,C-D,… K windows in one job, one Pythia each, event i in window i mod K; no background is shared. Use a multiple of K events --parton-ymax Y, --parton-y-mode {both,any} off, both regenerate the event until the two outgoing partons of the hard scattering have |y| < Y; cross sections corrected by the acceptance --b-min, --b-max 0, 3 fm the impact-parameter range (centrality) --sqrts 200 GeV the collision energy (the parameters are tuned at 200 GeV) --bulk-hadrons N 0 iSS in the job, N oversamples per event --no-particlize, --no-hydro-file, --no-jet-hadrons leave out the particlize file, the hydro file, the jet hadrons --eta-max, --charged, --no-x, --keep-bits-p/-x store less, as for hadronize.py, on both in-job hadron files --keep-primaries N with --bulk-hadrons: also the undecayed bulk hadrons of the first N oversamples, for SMASH later --colour-closure MODE the XML's (reconnect) how iColored closes colour lines that end in the medium: reconnect, reconnect_global, thermal, fake, none --matter-only Matter alone, no LBT and no recoils: a reference for colour studies --store-hadronization-input keep what was handed to Pythia, so rehadronize_jets.py can redo the jet hadrons later --no-subtraction the reference without the hard-momentum subtraction (counts the hard pair's energy twice, on purpose); keep it in its own OUTDIR --late-dtau 0 late step on MUSIC at a constant 0.02 fm/c; keep one setting per campaign --eloss-threads 0 -1: in parallel the final-state showers of an event run in parallel on OMP_NUM_THREADS threads (set it: unset means all cores per job): events ~13 % faster (GB10, 4 threads). 0 runs them serially, N on N threads. Serial and parallel give other showers for a seed, the thread count does not: one setting per campaign --max-skipped N 3 stop the job when more events fail

Choices that change the jets of a seed

X-SCAPE seeds each module from the order it was made. --bulk-hadrons and --no-hydro-file change that order, so the same seed gives other, equally valid jet showers (the hydro is identical). So do parallel showers, this driver's default, against --eloss-threads 0: every shower gets streams of its own (the thread count does not matter). Keep one choice per campaign if jets of different jobs are to be compared event by event; the files record it as prod_eloss_threads.

Before combining files, check the settings every file records (subtraction, b range, late time step, energy loss, colour closure): O+O analysis. Every option and the physics notes: the folder's README.

docs.title: Output and throughput
docs.text:
Each job writes (stem OO_isr_seedNNNN, or OO_isr_<campaign>_NNNN):

file content size per event <stem>_hadrons_jet_frag.h5 the jet hadrons (dijet, ISR emissions, Pythia's MPI partons, the hard pair's remnants), one unit per event, with the whole event record in units/ small <stem>_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5 the bulk, N oversamples per event ~13 kB per oversample <stem>_particlize.h5 MUSIC's freeze-out surface, the final partons, the initiators ~10 MB <stem>.h5 MUSIC's evolution (e, vx, vy, vz) on config/grid_oo.yaml (64 × 64 × 32, x, y ±9.84 fm), with diag/ per event ~17 MB <stem>.xml, .json, .log the job XML, the summary (cross sections, skipped events), the log

A module that throws inside an event costs that event only; the .json lists it under events_skipped.

Measured on 2 × RTX 3090 (24 cores), 8 jobs per GPU with 3 threads, MPS, MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC=block, 60 events per job:

output events/h per job disk per event hadron files only (--bulk-hadrons 10 --no-particlize --no-hydro-file) 13,728 1.43 GB 0.13 MB full outputs (hydro, particlize, jet hadrons) 12,700 1.40 GB 28 MB

The cores set the rate (~570 events/h per core). Full outputs write ~360 GB/h, more than an OSDF upload takes: use hadron files only, or a large local disk. On two GPUs, utils/launch_2gpu_oo.sh runs one container per GPU with these settings, and on SLURM PROD=oo selects this production in slurm_prod_array.sh: Clusters.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• O+O analysis: the per-event record, cross-section and N_coll weights, multiplicity, centrality, flow from the oversamples, jets.
  • prod_OO_isr/oo_isr_overview.ipynb: one job's medium and hadrons (needs Jupyter: the analysis venv or the container's xscape-jupyter).
  • Your first event: the same chain from Python with oo_workflow.py.

docs.title: Data on the OSDF
docs.text:
Productions are shared on the OSDF, the Open Science Data Federation of the OSG: a national network of data origins and caches, reached through the Pelican platform. Data sit on an origin under a namespace; clients ask a director for the closest cache and read from it with plain HTTP. For us that means: one place where a production made on a cluster, a workstation or a Mac can go, from which anyone can download it, or read just the part of a file they need without downloading it, from any machine and without an account. js-contrib's namespace is osdf:///fno4hic. Reading it is public; writing needs a login.

What is there

Today the namespace holds example and test productions. In the future, besides the example files, training data sets (for the ML/FNO surrogates) and physics simulation productions will be made available there.

The test data named in this documentation:

path content test/AuAu_0_10_jet_pth10-40_eta06_c1/ the ROOT files of an Au+Au jet campaign (pT̂ 10–40 GeV, 68 files, 2.1 GB), with its campaign file test/h5_read_test/ a small Au+Au hadron file, to try reading in place test/OO_test/ the hadron files of an O+O oo_workflow run, read in place by the notebook pythonic/oo_analysis.ipynb LHC/zjet_viz/ two Pb+Pb Z+jet events with their full hydro evolution (pair file, 0.93 GB), hadron files and movies: the example for 3D visualization of the medium and the jet wake RHIC/AuAu_dijet_viz/ one Au+Au 0–10 % dijet event (p̂T 30–40 GeV) with its full hydro evolution (pair file, 233 MB), hadron files and four movies: the example for full_event_pyvista.py, from the colliding nuclei to the hadrons

docs.title: The transfer tool: js_osdf.py
docs.text:
utils/remote_transfer/js_osdf.py lists, downloads, uploads and removes whole productions, single files or patterns, and picks the files by kind. It runs from a js-contrib checkout and makes its own Python environment on its first run (in ~/.cache/js_osdf/venv; a python3 ≥ 3.9 with venv and access to PyPI, a few seconds), so it needs no conda env or venv of yours:

git clone https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib.git
cd js-contrib/utils/remote_transfer
./js_osdf.py ls                     # the namespace: one folder per production

Keep it next to transfer_core.py, which it imports. Every command takes remote names as NAME, osdf:///fno4hic/NAME or /fno4hic/NAME.

docs.title: On a Mac: the xscape wheel
docs.text:
The xscape wheel (0.2.0 or later) has the tool as a command, xscape-osdf, with the same commands and options, and upload_follow.py as xscape-upload-follow. They run in the wheel's environment, which has pelicanfs and google-crc32c: no checkout, no environment in ~/.cache/js_osdf, nothing to install.

source ~/.venvs/xscape-0.2.0/bin/activate
xscape-osdf ls test                                    # as ./js_osdf.py ls test below
xscape-osdf download AuAu_c1 --what h5 --to ~/data
xscape-osdf login                                      # once, for uploads
xscape-upload-follow ~/xscape/examples/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/out AuAu_c1 --follow

In the examples below, xscape-osdf stands for ./js_osdf.py on the Mac.

docs.title: Browsing
docs.text:
./js_osdf.py ls                                  # the top level
./js_osdf.py ls test                             # a folder
./js_osdf.py ls test -r                          # every file below it
./js_osdf.py ls AuAu_c1 --what h5                # a production's files of one kind, with sizes
./js_osdf.py du                                  # space per top-level folder, and the total
./js_osdf.py du AuAu_c1 -d 2 --sort size         # below a folder, two levels, largest first

AuAu_c1 stands for a production folder; ls shows what is there.

docs.title: Downloading
docs.text:
./js_osdf.py download AuAu_c1 --what h5 --to /scratch            # -> /scratch/AuAu_c1/
./js_osdf.py download AuAu_c1 --what root --to /scratch          # only the ROOT files
./js_osdf.py download 'AuAu_c1/*_000[1-5]_*' --to /scratch/few   # a pattern (quoted): a few jobs
./js_osdf.py download AuAu_c1 --what h5 --to /scratch --dry-run  # what would come, and how much

The kinds go by file name:

--what files for h5 <stem>_particlize.h5, <stem>_hadrons_*.h5, the hadronization logs the hadron analyses: HadronFileReader needs the particlize files next to the hadron files, and h5 brings them along root <stem>_hadrons.root, <campaign>_campaign.root ROOT analyses alone: complete on their own pair <stem>.h5, the hydro (~0.17–0.29 GB per event), with its .json, .xml, .log the hydro, the wake observables, FNO training all (default) everything in the folder
  • Resumable and checked. Files already there with the same size and CRC32C are skipped, so an interrupted download finishes when the command runs again. Each file is written as <file>.part and renamed only when its size and checksum are right.
  • Where they go: a folder to --to/<folder>/, files and patterns to --to/<file>.
  • -j N transfers N files at once (default 4). Measured: ~69 MB/s down from a workstation.
  • --what takes a comma list (h5,root).

docs.title: Reading files in place
docs.text:
In the analysis environment (pelicanfs is installed by default), in the production container and in the xscape wheel (from 0.2.0), osdf:// paths can be read without downloading: pelicanfs finds a cache for the path and reads by byte ranges, so only the parts asked for travel. Both examples read public test files and run as they are:

import uproot
c = uproot.open("osdf:///fno4hic/test/AuAu_0_10_jet_pth10-40_eta06_c1/pth10-40_eta06_c1_campaign.root")
sigma = c["windows"].arrays(["sigma_mb"], library="np")["sigma_mb"]   # the pT-hat windows' cross sections

import fsspec, h5py, hdf5plugin                   # hdf5plugin: the Blosc filter of the HDF5 files
fs = fsspec.filesystem("osdf")
with fs.open("/fno4hic/test/h5_read_test/AuAu_0_10_jet_st1_t000_0001_hadrons_bulk_jet.h5", "rb",
             cache_type="blockcache", block_size=2**20) as fo, h5py.File(fo, "r") as f:
    so = f["hadrons/sample_offsets"][:]
    p = f["hadrons/p"][so[3]:so[4]]               # one oversample's momenta (E, px, py, pz)
  • Pass cache_type="blockcache", block_size=2**20 for HDF5: fsspec's default read-ahead re-fetches overlapping ranges when HDF5 jumps back to its metadata. With 1 MB blocks, one oversample of a 100 MB hadron file moved 6.3 MB instead of 31.5 MB.
  • Time: the first open in a process takes ~1–1.5 s (pelicanfs finds a cache); after that, one oversample ~0.1–0.2 s.
  • When to download instead: for whole productions and for anything read more than once (in place, every pass goes over the network again). HadronFileReader, ParticlizeFile, run_h5toROOT.py and the analysis/ scripts take local paths only.
  • Inside the production container the pelican command line does the same for single files: pelican object get osdf:///fno4hic/… /work/….
  • AttributeError: 'Client' object has no attribute 'info' (or list_files): pelicanfs up to 1.5.0 does not work with aiowebdav2 1.x (released 2026-11-02), so environments installed since then cannot open osdf:// URLs in uproot or list folders. Fix: pip install "aiowebdav2<1". js-contrib's requirement files pin it.
  • A first, hands-on look at pelicanfs (browsing, uproot, h5py, downloading) is tutorial 01, section 2.

What the files hold and how to read them: What a production writes, Hadrons, ROOT and C++.

docs.title: Uploading
docs.text:
Writing to /fno4hic needs write access to the namespace: a browser login, or a bearer token. Whatever is uploaded can be read by everyone.

./js_osdf.py login              # once: prints a link; log in and approve in any browser
./js_osdf.py status             # who, the scopes, the time left of the token and the login
./js_osdf.py upload /data/AuAu_c1 --what h5 --dry-run       # what would go
./js_osdf.py upload /data/AuAu_c1 --what h5                 # -> osdf:///fno4hic/AuAu_c1/
./js_osdf.py upload /data/out --what root --as AuAu_pth10-40_v1   # another folder name
./js_osdf.py rm -r AuAu_c1 --dry-run                         # what would be removed
  • The login lasts 15 days (renewals don't extend it): log in again before a long run would pass that date. It is kept in ~/.config/js_osdf/web/ and used by every later command. logout revokes it. A bearer token works too (--token-file, $BEARER_TOKEN_FILE, …).
  • Uploads of a directory go to osdf:///fno4hic/[PREFIX/]<directory name>/ (--as NAME for another name, --prefix for a parent folder). Only the files directly in the directory are sent, not its subdirectories: upload gpu0/, gpu1/ or t000/, … one by one (with --as CAMPAIGN/gpu0) or use upload_follow.py below.
  • Unfinished files are left out: HDF5 files whose complete attribute is false (a job still writing) and *.part files.
  • Checked: Pelican reports sizes but no checksums, so after each upload js_osdf.py checks the size at the origin and records size and CRC32C in a manifest in the remote folder; downloads are checked against it. Don't run two uploads into the same folder at once.
  • rm asks first (--yes doesn't; --dry-run lists all). Removed files can't be brought back.

Measured: ~80 MB/s up from a workstation, 4 or 8 files at once alike.

docs.title: Uploading while a production runs
docs.text:
A campaign can write faster than a local disk holds. utils/upload_follow.py uploads each job as soon as its <stem>.json says complete and, if asked, deletes the local copies after a verified upload, so the local disk no longer limits the campaign:

utils/upload_follow.py /data/AuAu_a AuAu_a                      # one pass, upload only
utils/upload_follow.py /data/AuAu_a AuAu_a --follow --delete pair   # while the campaign runs
touch /data/AuAu_a/.upload_final       # when the campaign is done: a last pass, then it exits
option --delete none (default) / pair / all after a verified upload, delete nothing / <stem>.h5 (the hydro) / also <stem>_particlize.h5 --keep-free SIZE with pair/all: delete only while the disk has less than SIZE free, the oldest uploads first --verify-every N before deleting, download every Nth file and compare it byte by byte (default 20; 0: never) --follow repeat every --interval s (default 60) until OUTBASE/.upload_final appears or --follow-pid ends
  • Verified means: the origin holds a file of the local size, the manifest's CRC32C matches the local file, and every Nth file was downloaded and compared. The .json, .log and .xml files are never deleted (run_jobs.sh needs the .json to skip finished jobs).
  • It runs on the host, next to Docker or on a node that sees a SLURM campaign's directories, from a js-contrib checkout (on a Mac with the xscape wheel: xscape-upload-follow, no checkout); any directory of run_jobs.sh output directories works (OUTBASE/<sub>/ → REMOTE/<sub>/). Its state survives restarts (OUTBASE/upload_state.json, log in OUTBASE/upload.log).
  • With launch_2gpu.sh, --upload REMOTE --delete pair starts it with the campaign (Clusters). launch_2gpu.sh --upload refuses to start without a login.
  • Hadronization output is uploaded afterwards: js_osdf.py upload OUTBASE/gpu0 --as REMOTE/gpu0 --what h5,root.

What to move where. The particlize files are self-contained (surfaces, partons, shower initiators), so hadronization on another cluster and the analysis need only --what h5; the large pair files (--what pair) only go where the hydro is used, e.g. FNO training.

docs.title: Google Cloud Storage
docs.text:
js_gcs.py, next to js_osdf.py, has the same commands and options for a Google Cloud Storage bucket (default gs://test_fno). The bucket is not public: reading and writing need a service-account JSON key (--key-file, $JS_GCS_KEY_FILE or $GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS). The analysis environment reads gs:// paths with --with-gcs.

./js_gcs.py upload /data/AuAu_a --what pair -j 8     # -> gs://test_fno/AuAu_a/
./js_gcs.py download AuAu_a --what root --to /scratch

On a Mac with the xscape wheel the command is xscape-gcs. Unlike xscape-osdf it keeps its own environment in ~/.cache/js_gcs (google-cloud-storage is not in the wheel), made on its first run.

All options, credentials and the tests: utils/remote_transfer/README.md.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Analysis environment: the venv that reads these files, with pelicanfs; on a Mac the xscape wheel reads them too.
  • Notebooks: oo_analysis.ipynb streams the O+O test files from the OSDF.

docs.title: Z+jet and other collision systems
docs.text: The physics of a production is in its user XML, so a new collision system or a different hard process is mostly a copy of an XML with a few lines changed. This page covers the two cases that already exist: the Z+jet production in Pb+Pb at 5.02 TeV, made for the CMS and ATLAS Z–hadron and Z+jet measurements, and Pb+Pb jets at the LHC from your own XML, with the steps to take for any other system. O+O and Ne+Ne at 5.36 TeV, and the event's other hard scatterings, which matter at the LHC, are on Extra hard scatterings. Both run through the Au+Au jet production's driver run_prod_jet.py, so everything in Au+Au jets applies. At the end, the production wizard plans the launch command for any of the productions.

docs.title: Z+jet in Pb+Pb at 5.02 TeV
docs.text:
The Z+jet production runs Pb+Pb collisions at √s_NN = 5.02 TeV, 0–30 %, with a hard process that makes a Z boson decaying to e⁺e⁻ or μ⁺μ⁻ and a recoiling parton. The Z's leptons pass through the medium untouched, so the Z tags the initial jet momentum; the recoil jet loses energy and leaves a wake. The inputs are in example/config/ (in the image: /opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/config):

  • PbPb_0_30_ZJet.xml: the Pb+Pb jet XML at 0–30 % (b_max 8.57 fm) with a Z+jet <PythiaGun> (Z + parton processes, Z → ee/μμ, <trigger>Z);
  • grid_PbPb.yaml: the larger Pb+Pb output grid (80 × 80 × 40 cells, x, y ±15.3 fm), for the edge flags;
  • hadronize.xml: the shared hadronization settings; its eCMforHadronization is set to the collision's 5020 GeV from the XML's PythiaGun automatically.

docs.title: The settings
docs.text:
The campaigns use six pT̂ windows with 4 jets per window per background (24 events per background), the Z's leptons inside the detector acceptance, and hadron files made in the job:

option --user-xml …/PbPb_0_30_ZJet.xml --grid …/grid_PbPb.yaml the Z+jet XML and the Pb+Pb grid --pthat-bins 20-30,30-35,35-45,45-55,55-70,70-200 --jets-per-bin 4 the windows: the p_T^Z > 40 GeV cross section is spread evenly over them, so little is lost to the window weights --lepton-ptmin 20 --lepton-etamax 2.5 both leptons p_T > 20 GeV, |η| < 2.5 (the CMS and ATLAS Z–hadron cuts); failing events are regenerated before any hydro, and the cross sections corrected --hadrons-only --oversample 40 --n-frag 40 --correlated hadron files only, 40 correlated samples per jet event --eta-max 2.6 --no-x --hadron-keep-bits-p 12 --hadron-keep-bits-x 8 --keep-primaries 0 all final particles at |η| < 2.6, no positions, rounded TAG_PREFIX=PbPb_0_30_seed (environment) names the files PbPb_0_30_<campaign>_… instead of AuAu_0_10_jet_…

--trigger Z comes from the XML; --trigger-ymax Y would add a Z rapidity cut (the campaigns apply |y_Z| offline). There is no cut on the recoiling parton.

The event's other hard scatterings. A 0–30 % Pb+Pb event has ~8 other hard scatterings above 15 GeV (the XML's <extraHard><pTHatMin>). Add --extra-hard to the options above to have them: their fragments then form the B of the Z+jet analysis as CMS's minimum-bias events do, and the Z, its recoil and the background stay bit-identical for the same seed. See Extra hard scatterings and, for the analyses, Jets with FastJet.

A current image

The Z trigger, --hadrons-only and TAG_PREFIX need an image built from the current code. Check it first: python run_prod_jet.py --help must list --trigger, and a --dry-run must print trigger Z (lepton pT > 20 GeV, lepton |eta| < 2.5), EOS 91 and eCMforHadronization 5020. Pin the image by digest for the campaign.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Check with --dry-run inside the image (no GPU work), then run. In Docker:

IMG=jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126                      # pinned by digest for a campaign
D=/opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/config
mkdir -p ~/prod/lbt_cache
docker run -d --name zjet --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -e TAG_PREFIX=PbPb_0_30_seed -e OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 -e OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive \
  -e MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC=block -e LBT_TABLE_CACHE=/work/lbt_cache/lbt_tables_v1.bin \
  -v "$HOME/prod:/work" $IMG \
  ./run_jobs.sh -j 3 --stagger 12 --campaign zjet_test 10 96 0 /work/zjet_test \
    --user-xml $D/PbPb_0_30_ZJet.xml --grid $D/grid_PbPb.yaml \
    --pthat-bins 20-30,30-35,35-45,45-55,55-70,70-200 --jets-per-bin 4 \
    --lepton-ptmin 20 --lepton-etamax 2.5 \
    --hadrons-only --oversample 40 --n-frag 40 --correlated \
    --eta-max 2.6 --no-x --hadron-keep-bits-p 12 --hadron-keep-bits-x 8 --keep-primaries 0

The liquefier's frame. PbPb_0_30_ZJet.xml doesn't set <CausalLiquefier><frame>, so the build's default applies. - Published campaigns (zjet_c00…, images from before 2026-11) were made in the lab frame. At the LHC that frame moves the wake of forward partons toward midrapidity: +19 % at |η_s| < 1 (The physics). - A newer image runs the Bjorken frame by default. Add --liquefier-frame lab to extend an old campaign, or bjorken/fluid for a new one. - Use a fresh output directory per frame: run_jobs.sh skips completed jobs whatever frame made them. - Never combine campaigns made in different frames in one analysis.

Ten jobs of 96 events (4 backgrounds each), three at a time: a Pb+Pb Z+jet job peaks at 14–16 GB of host memory (2.1× an Au+Au job; measured on the GB10), mostly MUSIC's larger box. It takes 2.1× the time of an Au+Au jet job and writes 1.7× the disk.

The scripts of the published campaigns are in utils/zjet/: ten campaigns zjet_c00 … zjet_c09 of 9,600 events each (100 jobs × 96 events), with disjoint seed ranges (campaign C uses seeds from 1 + 1000 C), so campaigns from different machines combine. Run them from a js-contrib checkout:

script runs zjet_slurm_campaign.sh one campaign as a SLURM array through utils/slurm_prod_array.sh: C=0 sbatch zjet_slurm_campaign.sh (set up for NCSA Delta's A40 nodes, 3 jobs per GPU; edit the #SBATCH lines for your site). C=0 NJOBS=1 is a ~1,000-event smoke test zjet_3090_campaign.sh one campaign on a two-GPU workstation through utils/launch_2gpu.sh: IMAGE=… ./zjet_3090_campaign.sh 0 zjet_3090_test.sh before the first campaign on a workstation: info (digest, commits, dry run), bench 3, bench 4, report, smoke

After each campaign: utils/check_deposition.py OUTDIR (Clusters), then the upload to the OSDF (Data on the OSDF).

docs.title: The pp reference
docs.text:
prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/run_prod_vacuum.py runs the same XML's PythiaGun and Matter in vacuum (no initial state, hydro, LBT or liquefier), with Colorless hadronization at the PythiaGun's energy. It runs on the CPU, ~0.02 s per event on the GB10, so 12,000 events take minutes:

python run_prod_vacuum.py --events 12000 --seed 900001 --campaign zjet_pp \
  --user-xml $D/PbPb_0_30_ZJet.xml --pthat-bins 20-30,30-35,35-45,45-55,55-70,70-200 \
  --lepton-ptmin 20 --lepton-etamax 2.5 \
  --n-frag 40 --eta-max 2.6 --no-x --hadron-keep-bits-p 12 --outdir /work/zjet_pp

It writes one <stem>_hadrons_jet_frag.h5 (attribute vacuum), read like the Pb+Pb jet files. Give it seeds of its own: the Pb+Pb campaigns' seeds would give the same Pythia events.

docs.title: What to know in the files
docs.text:
• The Z per event is in units/ of the hadron files (z_pt, z_y, z_phi, z_m, lep{1,2}_{pid,pt,eta,phi}); every paper's p_T^Z and mass window is applied offline.
  • Weight every event by its n_coll (units/n_coll): the geometry is drawn with P(b) ∝ b over 0–30 % and every event has one Z, while Z production scales with N_coll. Weight also by the window's cross section.
  • The two leptons are among the jet hadrons (jet_frag, pid ±11/±13) and in initiators/: remove them before a track or jet analysis.
  • Every background has its event plane near φ = 0 (3dMCGlauber puts the impact parameter along x). The means of a Z-frame analysis are unaffected; event mixing needs each background rotated by a random angle, which the Z-analysis scripts do by default.

The Z–hadron and Z+jet analyses, step by step: analysis/zjet/ and Hadrons. The campaign design (windows, cuts, expected statistics): utils/zjet/README.md.

docs.title: Another collision system: Pb+Pb at the LHC
docs.text: run_prod_jet.py takes a copy of AuAu_MCGlauber_MUSIC_0_10_jet.xml with --user-xml, fills in the job and checks it. So another system or energy is a copy of the XML with the collision changed. Here: Pb+Pb at √s_NN = 5.02 TeV, 0–10 %; the same steps apply to other nuclei and energies.

docs.title: 1. The XML
docs.text:
where Au+Au 200 GeV Pb+Pb 5.02 TeV why <IS><MCGlauber><projectile>, <target> Au Pb <IS><MCGlauber><sqrts> 200 5020 <IS><MCGlauber><b_max> 4.7 fm 4.95 fm centrality comes from b inside X-SCAPE (cenMin/cenMax are ignored): the geometric 0–10 %, π b² = 0.1 × 7.7 b <IS><grid_max_x>, <grid_max_y> 15 20 MUSIC's grid: the fireball is larger and lives longer <IS><grid_max_z> 6 8 MUSIC's η_s range: the beam rapidity is 8.5 instead of 5.4 <Hard><PythiaGun><eCM> 200 5020 the pT̂ windows 10–40 GeV your choice --pthat-bins

eCMforHadronization follows the collision automatically, so the one hadronize.xml serves every system. From a js-contrib checkout:

mkdir -p xml
T=contribs/PyJetscape/example/config
sed -e 's#<projectile>Au</projectile>#<projectile>Pb</projectile>#' \
    -e 's#<target>Au</target>#<target>Pb</target>#' \
    -e 's#<sqrts>200</sqrts>#<sqrts>5020</sqrts>#' \
    -e 's#<b_max>4.7</b_max>#<b_max>4.95</b_max>#' \
    -e 's#<grid_max_x> 15 </grid_max_x>#<grid_max_x> 20 </grid_max_x>#' \
    -e 's#<grid_max_y> 15 </grid_max_y>#<grid_max_y> 20 </grid_max_y>#' \
    -e 's#<grid_max_z> 6  </grid_max_z>#<grid_max_z> 8  </grid_max_z>#' \
    -e 's#<eCM>200</eCM>#<eCM>5020</eCM>#' \
    $T/AuAu_MCGlauber_MUSIC_0_10_jet.xml > xml/PbPb_0_10_jet.xml
diff $T/AuAu_MCGlauber_MUSIC_0_10_jet.xml xml/PbPb_0_10_jet.xml     # 8 lines must differ

The result is already in example/config/ as PbPb_0_10_jet.xml, with grid_PbPb.yaml; use them as they are or as a start for another system.

What the driver checks (it refuses an XML that breaks the two-stage setup, before any event): exactly two <Hydro><MUSIC> blocks, MUSIC_1 (background) and MUSIC_2 (jet leg), all MUSIC settings in the first; the liquefier's <dtau> equal to MUSIC's starting step; a <Hard><PythiaGun> block; no <SoftParticlization>, <JetHadronization>, <Afterburner> or writers (the hadrons come from stage 2); an output grid inside MUSIC's grid.

Choices to make before a production:

  • The tune. The 3D MC-Glauber, viscosity, freeze-out and energy-loss parameters are those of the Au+Au 200 GeV production; none is tuned at the LHC. Check the bulk against data first (ALICE: dN_ch/dη at |η| < 0.5 is 1943 ± 54 at 0–5 % and 1587 ± 47 at 5–10 %).
  • Pythia's MPI. PythiaGun switches multi-parton interactions on, and every parton it hands over is showered and can deposit; at 5.02 TeV that is many more partons than at 200 GeV. PartonLevel:MPI = off in <LinesToRead> leaves the hard process and its ISR.
  • The output grid. The default grid (±12.2 fm) fits, but the jet leg can reach its edge: grid_PbPb.yaml is larger with the same cells (files of different grids don't go into one training set).
  • Names. TAG_PREFIX=PbPb_0_10_seed names the files PbPb_0_10_… (letters, digits, ., _, -, ending in _seed; one per OUTDIR), or put the system into the campaign name.

docs.title: 2. Your XML from outside the container
docs.text:
The XML doesn't need to be in the image. Bind its directory and give the driver the path as the container sees it, as an absolute path:

bind then Docker -v "$PWD/xml:/xml:ro" --user-xml /xml/PbPb_0_10_jet.xml Apptainer --bind "$PWD/xml:/xml", or nothing for a file under $HOME --user-xml /xml/PbPb_0_10_jet.xml SLURM (slurm_prod_array.sh, slurm_hadronize.sh) BINDS="$PWD/xml:/xml" in EXTRA_ARGS (stage 1) or HAD_ARGS (stage 2)

The same holds for --grid, --main-xml and --hadronize-xml. The file is read when a job starts, and each job stores the XML it ran (<stem>.xml, prod_user_xml): don't edit it during a campaign.

docs.title: 3. A first event, then the campaign
docs.text:
# in the container (Apptainer; Docker with -v "$PWD/xml:/xml:ro" -v "$PWD/prod:/work")
PROD=/opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet
apptainer exec --nv --env MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC=block --pwd "$PROD" \
  --bind "$PWD/xml:/xml,$SCRATCH/prod:/work" xscape_prod.sif \
  python run_prod_jet.py --user-xml /xml/PbPb_0_10_jet.xml --events 3 --seed 1 \
    --write-particlize both --outdir /work/PbPb_test --out PbPb_0_10_jet_seed0001.h5 --dry-run
# ... the same without --dry-run, then stage 2
apptainer exec --pwd "$PROD" --bind "$PWD/xml:/xml,$SCRATCH/prod:/work" xscape_prod.sif \
  ./run_hadronize.py /work/PbPb_test -j 3 --oversample 100 --n-frag 20

One event against Au+Au, measured on the GB10 (one job alone, pT̂ 50–70 GeV, --write-particlize both, default output grid, 100 oversamples):

Pb+Pb 5.02 TeV Au+Au 200 GeV wall time of the event (both legs) 38.9 s 17.1 s peak host memory of the job 15.7 GB 6.1 GB freeze-out cells per leg 2.55 M 1.0 M showers, droplets, deposited energy 18, 74, 336 GeV 2, 25, 32 GeV pair file, particlize file 321 MB, 395 MB 245 MB, 155 MB hadron file per leg (100 oversamples) 79 MB 19 MB dN_ch/dη, |η| < 0.5, background 1534 ± 4 (ALICE 0–10 %: ~1765) 577 ± 2

The campaign is the Au+Au one with the XML (and the grid) passed after OUTDIR:

DockerSLURM 
docker run -d --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -e OMP_NUM_THREADS=3 -e OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive -e MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC=block \
  -e LBT_TABLE_CACHE=/work/lbt_cache/lbt_tables_v1.bin \
  -v "$PWD/xml:/xml:ro" -v "$HOME/prod:/work" $IMG \
  ./run_jobs.sh -j 4 --stagger 12 --campaign PbPb_c1 20 15 0 /work/PbPb_c1 \
    --user-xml /xml/PbPb_0_10_jet.xml --grid /xml/grid_PbPb.yaml \
    --pthat-bins 40-60,60-80,80-100 --jets-per-bin 5 --parton-ymax 0.6 --write-particlize both

# stage 1: ~16 GB per job, so fewer jobs per GPU than for Au+Au
SIF=$PWD/xscape_prod.sif CAMPAIGN=PbPb_c1 P=5 BINDS="$PWD/xml:/xml" \
  EXTRA_ARGS="--user-xml /xml/PbPb_0_10_jet.xml --grid /xml/grid_PbPb.yaml --pthat-bins 40-60,60-80,80-100 --jets-per-bin 5 --parton-ymax 0.6 --write-particlize both" \
  sbatch --array=0-19 --cpus-per-task=20 --mem=96G utils/slurm_prod_array.sh
# stage 2
SIF=$PWD/xscape_prod.sif CAMPAIGN=PbPb_c1 \
  HAD_ARGS="--oversample 200 --n-frag 50 --keep-bits-p 12 --keep-bits-x 8" \
  sbatch --array=0-19 --mem=48G utils/slurm_hadronize.sh
  • Memory: plan ~16 GB per job, 4–5 jobs on 96 GB; measure events/h with a short sweep of P on the first node.
  • Disk: ~0.7 GB per event with a new background every event; a background shared by 15 jets saves most of the background's share. Hadrons are ~4× Au+Au per oversample, so 200 oversamples give the statistics of 400–500 in Au+Au.
  • Stage 2 memory: ~2.3 GB per process at 100 oversamples.
  • Hydro-only Pb+Pb (prod_AuAu_0_10/run_prod.py) takes the same <IS> changes in a copy of its XML.

Here the grid is bound from xml/: copy grid_PbPb.yaml there, or pass the image's own path. Full details: docs/README_2stage.md, §9.

docs.title: Planning a production: the wizard
docs.text:
utils/prodwizard.py plans a campaign before anything runs. Pick a production preset and a machine; it writes the launch command with the settings measured for that machine (launch_2gpu.sh on a two-GPU workstation, run_jobs.sh on a single machine or Mac, slurm_prod_array.sh on a cluster) and estimates events/h, duration, disk and memory, each marked as measured or estimated with its source. It checks the plan: events per job a multiple of the pT̂ windows × jets, memory, disk, upload rate, the image, the campaign name. It never starts jobs.

utils/prodwizard.py --list                 # presets and machines
utils/prodwizard.py --preset auau_jet --machine 2x3090 --events 2700 --campaign c5 --out /data/c5
utils/prodwizard.py --preset pbpb_zjet --machine slurm_a40 --events 19200 --gpus 20 \
    --campaign zjet_c10 --save launch_zjet_c10.sh      # a script, the plan in its header
utils/prodwizard.py                        # the interactive wizard: a form, the plan beside it
presets (--preset) auau_jet Au+Au jets, pair + particlize files (the campaign setting) auau_particlize_only Au+Au jets, particlize file only auau_hadrons_only Au+Au jets, hadron files only, in the job oo_hadrons, oo_full O+O with ISR: hadron files only; or the default outputs pbpb_zjet Pb+Pb 5.02 TeV 0–30 % Z+jet, hadron files only

The machines (--machine) are 2x3090, gb10, m3max and SLURM nodes with one slurm_v100, slurm_a40, slurm_a100 or slurm_l40s per array task; further options set --events-per-job, --image, --first-seed, --jobs-per-gpu, --omp, --upload, --delete and --min-free. The command-line mode needs only the standard library; the interactive wizard needs textual (in the analysis venv), and runs in a browser with textual serve "utils/prodwizard.py". The presets and measured rates are in utils/prod_presets.json.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
The other sections of this site are a reference, organized by topic. The tutorials are a path through it instead: step-by-step Jupyter notebooks that start with nothing installed and end with your own analysis and your own modules. Each tutorial:

  • states its goal, its time, what it needs, and its data and their size;
  • explains the physics behind each step, linked to The physics;
  • has numbered steps you run yourself;
  • ends with a check your result cell, which compares against the expected numbers, and with exercises and links to the reference pages.

The notebooks run on your own computer: in the production container, with the xscape wheel on a Mac, or in the analysis environment. The analysis tutorials also run in Google Colab. The pages here show them with their outputs. To run them, see Setting up.

The outputs shown were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal. A notebook that needed something else says so at its top. Where a tutorial reads fixed example files, your numbers should match the ones shown. Where it runs X-SCAPE, they can differ slightly from setup to setup.

Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics results

The tutorials and their analyses are work in progress and need further vetting. They are meant mainly as examples of how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small (one background with five jets, a hundred-odd events, a few O+O events), so the statistics are low, and the definitions and procedures have not been checked to the standard of a publication. Treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result, and see the note on the analysis section.

docs.title: PyJetscape
docs.text:
# tutorial needs status Set up and run 01 Check your setup: what your setup can do, the data, a first file and plot any setup ready 02 Your first events in Python: three O+O events with the Pythonic interface, the stages of an event, its partons and hadrons; X-SCAPE: the production container or the Mac wheel (or a source build). Analysis: any setup, Colab included. Tutorial 01 tells you which tutorials run where you are. The advanced tutorials (later) follow once the comparisons with measured data have been tested further; until then the tutorials compare the model only with itself (jet against background, Au+Au against p+p).

docs.title: The data
docs.text: The tutorials read example files from the OSDF with pelicanfs, the OSDF's client for Python, with no account needed (tutorial 01 introduces it). The files are streamed as they are read, or downloaded once with get_data.py; see Setting up. The data sets and their contents are listed in datasets.json.

docs.title: Other contribs
docs.text: The tutorials live in tutorials/<contrib>/ in the repository, one folder per contrib. Tutorials for FastHydro and the visualization can follow the same layout.

docs.title: Setting up the tutorials
docs.text:
The tutorials are Jupyter notebooks that you run on your own computer, in a setup you may already have: the production container, the xscape wheel on a Mac, or the analysis environment. They work with the releases already out. Everything a tutorial needs, apart from the setup itself, comes with the tutorials or is fetched by them.

setup runs X-SCAPE the hydro runs on the analysis tutorials install production container yes an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA), when passed in yes Production container, images from 2026-10-28 on Mac, xscape wheel yes the Apple Silicon GPU (Metal), by default yes Mac (xscape wheel), 0.2.0 or later analysis environment no – yes Analysis environment Google Colab no – yes nothing: open a notebook from GitHub

ROOT's C++ (tutorial 10) needs a ROOT installation next to the setup, for example from conda or, on a Mac, from Homebrew (ROOT and C++). Neither the container nor the wheel brings ROOT.

docs.title: 1. Get the tutorials
docs.text:
In a checkout of js-contrib, they are in tutorials/pyjetscape/. Without one, download them with curl:

A releaseThe main branch 
curl -L https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/releases/download/tutorials-v2/pyjetscape-tutorials.tar.gz | tar xz

A release (tutorials-vN) is fixed, and goes with a fixed version of the data: tutorials-v2 reads the data in tutorials/v2/ on the OSDF.

mkdir pyjetscape-tutorials && curl -L https://codeload.github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/tar.gz/refs/heads/main \
  | tar xz -C pyjetscape-tutorials --strip-components=3 js-contrib-main/tutorials/pyjetscape

The latest version. This downloads the whole repository (about 20 MB) and unpacks only the tutorials.

Both commands create a folder pyjetscape-tutorials/. Later releases of the container and the wheel will also carry the tutorials.

docs.title: 2. Start Jupyter
docs.text:
Production containerMac (xscape wheel)Analysis environmentGoogle Colab

Download the tutorials on the host, into the directory you mount (the image has wget but not curl). Then start JupyterLab in the image with xscape-jupyter:

mkdir -p work && (cd work && curl -L https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/releases/download/tutorials-v2/pyjetscape-tutorials.tar.gz | tar xz)
docker run --rm -it --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -p 8888:8888 \
  -v "$PWD/work:/work" jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 xscape-jupyter /work/pyjetscape-tutorials

Open the http://127.0.0.1:8888/lab?token=... line it prints.

  • --gpus all passes the NVIDIA GPU in. MUSIC runs on it with CUDA; without it, MUSIC runs on its CPU path, about 10 times slower. The analysis tutorials need no GPU, so leave it out on a computer without one.
  • Apptainer on a cluster: apptainer exec --nv --bind "$PWD/work:/work" xscape_prod.sif xscape-jupyter /work/pyjetscape-tutorials, with an ssh tunnel to the node (Jupyter in the container).
  • Images older than 2026-10-28 have no Jupyter: pull a newer one.
source ~/.venvs/xscape-0.2.0/bin/activate      # the line install.sh printed
jupyter lab pyjetscape-tutorials

JupyterLab opens in your browser. The wheel runs the hydro on the Apple Silicon GPU, by default, through Metal; there is nothing to switch on. When an event starts, MUSIC prints [MUSIC-GPU] Metal device: <your chip>. Run Jupyter natively in Terminal: inside a virtual machine or a container there is no Metal GPU, and MUSIC falls back to the CPU.

source ~/.venvs/js_analysis/bin/activate
jupyter lab pyjetscape-tutorials

For VS Code or a JupyterLab of another environment, register the environment as a kernel (setup_analysis_env.sh --kernel js_analysis) and choose it in the notebook.

Open a tutorial from its page here or on GitHub with the Open in Colab badge at its top. The first cell fetches the tutorial helpers and installs the jetscape readers with the analysis packages, which takes about a minute. Colab runs the analysis tutorials; it cannot run X-SCAPE. Its sessions are temporary, so the installation and any downloaded data are gone the next time.

Then open 01_check_setup.ipynb. It names your setup, says where the hydro would run, checks that the data can be reached, reads a first file and lists the tutorials that run here.

docs.title: 3. The data
docs.text:
The tutorials read example files from the OSDF, in the public namespace /fno4hic, with pelicanfs, the OSDF's client for Python. It asks the OSDF director which caches hold a file, reads from the nearest one, and moves on to the next when a cache fails. No account is needed. When a notebook opens a file, it takes the local copy if there is one, and otherwise streams only the parts it reads, as an osdf:// URL. Tutorial 01 introduces pelicanfs; Data on the OSDF has the rest.

Every setup has pelicanfs: the container, the Mac wheel and the analysis environment, and in Colab the first cell installs it. Where it is missing (the pure-Python pyjetscape wheel 0.2.0), the tutorials read the same caches over plain HTTPS, with the standard library.

To download a set once, for working offline or for the large files (the hydro pairs are 0.2–0.9 GB each), run get_data.py in the tutorial folder:

python get_data.py --list                          # the sets, their sizes and contents
python get_data.py oo_test auau_jet_event          # -> data/oo_test/, data/auau_jet_event/
python get_data.py auau_hadrons_root --max-files 3 # the first three files of a large set
  • get_data.py downloads with pelicanfs, and over plain HTTPS where pelicanfs is missing, so it runs in every setup, inside the container too.
  • It takes the file names and sizes from the manifest that each OSDF folder holds, and checks every file's size. It also checks the CRC32C checksum when google-crc32c or crc32c is installed.
  • Interrupted downloads resume where they stopped.
  • To keep the data elsewhere, use --to DIR and set JS_TUTORIAL_DATA=DIR for the notebooks.

The tutorials' data sets (a complete Au+Au pair set, a hadron-level Au+Au campaign in three p̂T windows, its p+p reference, a small O+O campaign) are in osdf:///fno4hic/tutorials/v2/; data_recipes/make_v2.sh in the tutorial folder says how each was made. They will never be overwritten, so a tutorial release and its data stay together.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: problem cause and fix OSError: Can't synchronously read data (can't open directory .../hdf5/lib/plugin) the files are compressed with Blosc and h5py has no filter for it: import hdf5plugin before reading. The tutorials' first cell does this (te.setup()). the OSDF is not reachable a firewall or proxy blocks osdf-director.osg-htc.org. Download the data elsewhere with get_data.py and copy the data/ folder. note: pelicanfs ... does not work with aiowebdav2 1.x; reading over HTTPS instead an environment installed after 2026-11-02 has aiowebdav2 1.x, with which pelicanfs (up to 1.5.0) cannot list or stat files, so uproot.open("osdf://...") fails. The tutorials read over HTTPS then; to fix the environment: pip install "aiowebdav2<1". ModuleNotFoundError: _common the notebook was started outside its folder. Start Jupyter in the tutorial folder, or open the notebook from there. the container's Jupyter page does not load Docker: -p 8888:8888 is missing. Apptainer: tunnel to the compute node, not the login node. MUSIC prints Metal init failed, falling back to CPU the Mac wheel runs in a virtual machine or a container: run it natively in Terminal.

The GPU. The hydrodynamic evolution is the most expensive step of an event, and js-contrib runs it on the GPU with MUSIC4GPU. There are two builds:

  • The Mac wheel uses the Apple Silicon GPU by default, through Metal: there is nothing to switch on. When an event starts, MUSIC prints [MUSIC-GPU] Metal device: <your chip>. It falls back to the CPU only where there is no Metal GPU, inside a virtual machine or a container; run natively in Terminal instead.
  • The production container uses an NVIDIA GPU through CUDA, but only one that Docker (--gpus all) or Apptainer (--nv) passes in. Without one, MUSIC runs on its CPU path, about 10 times slower.

The analysis tutorials need no GPU. How the GPU and CPU results compare: GPU acceleration.

hdf5plugin matters for every tutorial: the production files are compressed with Blosc, and without it h5py opens a file and lists its contents but cannot read a single dataset. te.setup() loads it for you.

             cache_type="blockcache", block_size=2**20) as fo, h5py.File(fo, "r") as f:
    pid = f["hadrons/pid"][:1000]

Streaming suits a first look and single parts of a file. A file you read in full, or more than once, is better downloaded.

Now the pseudorapidity \(\eta\) and the transverse momentum \(p_T\) of every hadron, and the event each hadron belongs to:

In [8]: Copied! 
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import CHARGED     # the |pid| of the charged hadrons (and e, mu)

pt = np.hypot(p[:, 1], p[:, 2])
ok = pt > 0                                    # eta is undefined along the beam axis
eta = np.full(len(pt), np.nan)
eta[ok] = np.arcsinh(p[ok, 3] / pt[ok])        # = -ln tan(theta/2), stable in float32
charged = np.isin(np.abs(pid), CHARGED)

n_events = len(units["event"])
n_samp = units["n_samples"]
per_event = np.diff(sample_off[unit_off])      # hadrons of each event, all oversamples
event_of = np.repeat(np.arange(n_events), per_event)
hadrons_per_sample = per_event / n_samp

The histograms are made with hist, the histogram package of Scikit-HEP, which every tutorial uses. Each axis has a name and a label. With .Weight() storage a histogram also keeps the sum of the squared weights, so it knows its statistical errors. Each hadron is weighted by \(1/N_\text{oversamples}\) of its event, which gives yields per oversample: one sampling of the event.

The charged-hadron multiplicity at midrapidity, \(dN_{ch}/d\eta\) for \(|\eta| < 0.5\), is then a sum over the bins between \(-0.5\) and \(0.5\). hist.loc selects bins by value, and ::sum adds them up:

In [9]: Copied! 
import hist

h_eta = (hist.Hist.new
         .Integer(0, n_events, name="event", label="event")
         .Reg(48, -6, 6, name="eta", label=r"$\eta$")
         .Weight())
c = charged & ok
h_eta.fill(event=event_of[c], eta=eta[c], weight=1.0 / n_samp[event_of[c]])

mid = h_eta[:, hist.loc(-0.5):hist.loc(0.5):sum]     # |eta| < 0.5, one unit of eta wide
dnch_deta = mid.values()
for i in range(n_events):
    print(f"event {i}: {hadrons_per_sample[i]:.1f} hadrons per oversample, "
          f"dNch/deta(|eta|<0.5) = {dnch_deta[i]:.1f} +- {np.sqrt(mid.variances()[i]):.1f}")

What to notice.

  • The multiplicity is not set by the participants alone. Event 1 has fewer participants than event 0, but more hadrons at midrapidity. In the 3D initial state the energy is deposited along strings between the colliding nucleons, and their number and lengths fluctuate. With three events these fluctuations dominate; the trend with centrality appears over many events (tutorial 05).
  • The \(\eta\) distributions are lumpy and asymmetric, event by event. The strings break boost invariance: an event can have more hadrons at forward rapidity than at midrapidity (event 0). Averaged over many events, the distribution becomes smooth and symmetric. The 20 oversamples only reduce the sampling noise; they do not average over these fluctuations, since they all come from the same fluid.
  • Heavier hadrons peak at higher \(p_T\): pions near 0.3 GeV, kaons near 0.5 GeV, protons near 0.7 GeV. All hadrons leave the fluid with its local flow velocity, and at the same velocity a heavier hadron has more momentum. This radial flow shows up more clearly in Au+Au (tutorial 05).

docs.title: 01 · Check your setup¶
docs.text:
Time: 5 minutes · Needs: any of the setups below · Data: oo_test (1.5 MB) and a few kB of pp_ref, streamed

This first tutorial runs anywhere and checks four things:

  1. what your setup can do: run X-SCAPE, or only analyse files;
  2. how the example data are read from the OSDF, with pelicanfs, and whether they can be reached;
  3. whether a production file can be read, with a first plot from it;
  4. which of the following tutorials run here.

How to get the tutorials and start Jupyter (production container, Mac wheel, analysis environment, Colab) is on the setup page.

Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics. The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

The outputs shown were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal. That environment uses the X-SCAPE checkout, so it appears as the source setup below. Sections 1 and 4 describe that setup, and yours will differ there. Section 3 reads a fixed file, so your numbers there should match exactly.

docs.title: 1. What can this setup do?¶
docs.text:
The tutorials run in five setups. They differ in one main point: whether X-SCAPE itself can run, or only the readers of its files.

setup runs X-SCAPE the hydro (MUSIC) runs on ROOT (C++) how you got it container yes an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA), if the container sees one no the production image, xscape-jupyter mac-wheel yes the Apple Silicon GPU (Metal), by default no the xscape wheel on a Mac source yes the GPU it was built for if built with it a source build of X-SCAPE analysis no – if added (conda) the analysis environment, or the pyjetscape wheel colab no – no Google Colab, set up by the first cell

The line printed above names your setup. The table below lists what it has; gpu_hydro says where MUSIC runs.

docs.title: 2. The data on the OSDF¶
docs.text:
The example files live on the Open Science Data Federation (OSDF), in the public namespace /fno4hic. Reading them needs no account.

They are read with pelicanfs, the OSDF's client for Python. For each file it asks the OSDF director which caches hold it, reads from the nearest one, and moves on to the next cache when one fails. A file is named by its path in the federation, and osdf:// in front makes its URL:

osdf:///fno4hic/tutorials/v2/pp_ref/ppref_campaign.root

pelicanfs is an fsspec file system, so such URLs work wherever Python reads files through fsspec: in uproot, in h5py (through fs.open), in pandas. The production container, the Mac wheel and the analysis environment have it; in Colab the first cell installs it. Where it is missing, the tutorials read the same files over plain HTTPS.

First, can the OSDF be reached, and how?

docs.title: Browsing¶
docs.text: te.osdf() returns pelicanfs's file system, fsspec.filesystem("osdf"). Like a local file system, it lists folders. The tutorials' data sets are the folders below /fno4hic/tutorials/v2; pp_ref holds the files of a p+p reference production:

docs.title: Reading in place¶
docs.text: uproot opens an osdf:// URL like a local path, and fetches only the parts it reads, by byte ranges. The campaign file of pp_ref has a table windows with the cross section of each \(\hat p_T\) window of the production (tutorial 05 explains them):

docs.title: Downloading¶
docs.text:
To download a set, for working offline or for the larger files, run get_data.py in the tutorial folder (in a terminal, or here with !). It downloads with pelicanfs (over HTTPS where pelicanfs is missing), checks every file's size, and resumes interrupted downloads:

python get_data.py --list                 # the sets
python get_data.py oo_test                # -> data/oo_test/
python get_data.py auau_jet_event --to ~/xscape_data    # elsewhere; then set JS_TUTORIAL_DATA

JS_TUTORIAL_DATA tells the tutorials where the data folder is (default: data/ next to the notebooks).

In your own scripts, pelicanfs copies a file with fs.get("/fno4hic/.../file.h5", "file.h5"). For whole productions, uploads and protected namespaces, js-contrib has the transfer tool js_osdf.py (xscape-osdf with the Mac wheel). The website's page Data on the OSDF covers all of it, reading files in place included.

docs.title: 3. A first file¶
docs.text:
The set oo_test holds the hadrons of three O+O events at \(\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200\) GeV from the Pythonic workflow (tutorial 02 makes such files yourself). In each event:

  • a 3D MC-Glauber initial state with strings sets up the fluid,
  • MUSIC evolves it, and the freeze-out surface is found,
  • Cooper–Frye sampling (iSS) turns the surface into hadrons. The surface is sampled 20 times: 20 oversamples of the same event, which differ only by the sampling.

The file OO_workflow_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5 holds these bulk hadrons. All hadrons are in one flat table (hadrons/p, hadrons/pid, ...); unit_offsets and sample_offsets say where each event (unit) and each oversample starts. The table units/ has one row per event, with the Glauber impact parameter \(b\) and the numbers of participants and binary collisions.

docs.text: From what your setup has (section 1), here is what the tutorials need and whether they can run. Tutorials marked planned are still being written.

%%writefile out/02_first_events/oo_events.py
"""Run every event of a user XML with the Pythonic interface:  python oo_events.py XML NAME
Writes, next to the XML: NAME_hadrons_{bulk_bg,jet_frag}.h5, and NAME_events.json,
NAME_partons.npz, NAME_surface.npz with a few numbers, the final partons and a cut through
the freeze-out surface of each event."""
import json, sys, time
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import jetscape as js
from jetscape import pyjetscape_core as core
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronH5Writer
from jetscape.particlize_h5 import SURFACE_COLUMNS
from jetscape.records import initiator_rows

S = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(SURFACE_COLUMNS)}       # the columns of a surface cell


def glauber_record():
    """This event's geometry, from 3dMCGlauber's events_summary.dat in the working directory."""
    with open("events_summary.dat") as fh:
        rows = [ln.split() for ln in fh if ln.strip() and not ln.startswith("#")]
    _, npart, ncoll, nstrings, b = rows[-1][:5]
    return {"npart": int(npart), "ncoll": int(ncoll), "strings": int(nstrings), "b": float(b)}


def surface_flow(surf):
    """The transverse four-velocity u_T of each cell of a freeze-out surface, and the fluid
    volume that crosses the cell, |u^mu dSigma_mu|, as its weight."""
    u = surf[:, [S["u0"], S["u1"], S["u2"], S["u3"]]]
    dsig = surf[:, [S["ds0"], S["ds1"], S["ds2"], S["ds3"]]]
    return np.hypot(surf[:, S["u1"]], surf[:, S["u2"]]), np.abs(np.sum(u * dsig, axis=1))


def main(user_xml, name):
    out = Path(user_xml).resolve().parent
    n_os = int(ET.parse(user_xml).getroot().findtext("SoftParticlization/iSS/number_of_repeated_sampling"))
    rows, partons, cuts, t0 = [], {}, {}, time.time()
    with js.JobDir(out, user_xml, name=name) as job, \
         js.per_event(job.main_xml, job.user_xml) as driver:
        print("modules:", " -> ".join(t.GetId() + (f" ({', '.join(c.GetId() for c in t.GetTaskList())})"
                                                  if t.GetTaskList() else "")
                                      for t in driver.GetTaskList()))
        gun = next(t for t in driver.GetTaskList() if isinstance(t, core.HardProcess))
        hydro, mgr = driver.hydro, driver.energy_loss_manager
        iss, had = driver.soft_particlization, driver.hadronization_manager
        iss.use_compact_output()                         # iSS hands its hadrons over as arrays
        with HadronH5Writer(out / f"{name}_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5", tag="bulk_bg", n_samples=n_os) as bulk_w, \
             HadronH5Writer(out / f"{name}_hadrons_jet_frag.h5", tag="jet_frag", n_samples=1,
                            initiators=True) as jet_w:
            for i in driver.events():
                # ── this event's results, while it is in memory ──────────────────────
                record = {"pthat": gun.info["pthat"], **glauber_record()}
                surf = hydro.surface_to_numpy()          # the freeze-out surface
                fp = mgr.final_parton_array()            # the partons handed to hadronization
                bulk = iss.hadron_array()                # n_os oversamples
                jet = had.hadron_array()
                bulk_w.append_unit(bulk.to_dict(), unit=i, event=i, seed=iss.last_random_seed,
                                   n_cells=len(surf), **record)
                jet_w.append_unit(jet.to_dict(), initiators=initiator_rows(mgr.initiator_array()),
                                  unit=i, event=i, seed=had.last_random_seed, **record)
                partons[f"event{i}"] = fp
                mid = (np.abs(surf[:, S["eta"]]) < 0.15) & (np.abs(surf[:, S["y"]]) < 0.3)
                cuts[f"event{i}"] = surf[mid][:, [S["tau"], S["x"], S["u1"]]]   # through the middle
                uT, w = surface_flow(surf)
                cuts[f"event{i}_uT"] = np.histogram(uT, bins=40, range=(0, 1), weights=w)[0]
                rows.append({"event": i, **record, "cells": len(surf),
                             "tau_max": float(surf[:, S["tau"]].max()),
                             "flow_uT": float(np.sum(w * uT) / np.sum(w)),
                             "final partons": len(fp), "bulk hadrons / oversample": len(bulk) / n_os,
                             "jet hadrons": len(jet), "iSS seed": iss.last_random_seed})
                print(f"{name}: event {i} done, {time.time() - t0:.0f} s", flush=True)
    json.dump(rows, open(out / f"{name}_events.json", "w"), indent=1)
    np.savez(out / f"{name}_partons.npz", **partons)
    np.savez(out / f"{name}_surface.npz", **cuts)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])

the columns of a surface cell def glauber_record(): """This event's geometry, from 3dMCGlauber's events_summary.dat in the working directory.""" with open("events_summary.dat") as fh: rows = [ln.split() for ln in fh if ln.strip() and not ln.startswith("#")] _, npart, ncoll, nstrings, b = rows[-1][:5] return {"npart": int(npart), "ncoll": int(ncoll), "strings": int(nstrings), "b": float(b)} def surface_flow(surf): """The transverse four-velocity u_T of each cell of a freeze-out surface, and the fluid volume that crosses the cell, |u^mu dSigma_mu|, as its weight.""" u = surf[:, [S["u0"], S["u1"], S["u2"], S["u3"]]] dsig = surf[:, [S["ds0"], S["ds1"], S["ds2"], S["ds3"]]] return np.hypot(surf[:, S["u1"]], surf[:, S["u2"]]), np.abs(np.sum(u * dsig, axis=1)) def main(user_xml, name): out = Path(user_xml).resolve().parent n_os = int(ET.parse(user_xml).getroot().findtext("SoftParticlization/iSS/number_of_repeated_sampling")) rows, partons, cuts, t0 = [], {}, {}, time.time() with js.JobDir(out, user_xml, name=name) as job, \ js.per_event(job.main_xml, job.user_xml) as driver: print("modules:", " -> ".join(t.GetId() + (f" ({', '.join(c.GetId() for c in t.GetTaskList())})" if t.GetTaskList() else "") for t in driver.GetTaskList())) gun = next(t for t in driver.GetTaskList() if isinstance(t, core.HardProcess)) hydro, mgr = driver.hydro, driver.energy_loss_manager iss, had = driver.soft_particlization, driver.hadronization_manager iss.use_compact_output() # iSS hands its hadrons over as arrays with HadronH5Writer(out / f"{name}_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5", tag="bulk_bg", n_samples=n_os) as bulk_w, \ HadronH5Writer(out / f"{name}_hadrons_jet_frag.h5", tag="jet_frag", n_samples=1, initiators=True) as jet_w: for i in driver.events(): # ── this event's results, while it is in memory ────────────────────── record = {"pthat": gun.info["pthat"], **glauber_record()} surf = hydro.surface_to_numpy() # the freeze-out surface fp = mgr.final_parton_array() # the partons handed to hadronization bulk = iss.hadron_array() # n_os oversamples jet = had.hadron_array() bulk_w.append_unit(bulk.to_dict(), unit=i, event=i, seed=iss.last_random_seed, n_cells=len(surf), **record) jet_w.append_unit(jet.to_dict(), initiators=initiator_rows(mgr.initiator_array()), unit=i, event=i, seed=had.last_random_seed, **record) partons[f"event{i}"] = fp mid = (np.abs(surf[:, S["eta"]]) < 0.15) & (np.abs(surf[:, S["y"]]) < 0.3) cuts[f"event{i}"] = surf[mid][:, [S["tau"], S["x"], S["u1"]]] # through the middle uT, w = surface_flow(surf) cuts[f"event{i}_uT"] = np.histogram(uT, bins=40, range=(0, 1), weights=w)[0] rows.append({"event": i, **record, "cells": len(surf), "tau_max": float(surf[:, S["tau"]].max()), "flow_uT": float(np.sum(w * uT) / np.sum(w)), "final partons": len(fp), "bulk hadrons / oversample": len(bulk) / n_os, "jet hadrons": len(jet), "iSS seed": iss.last_random_seed}) print(f"{name}: event {i} done, {time.time() - t0:.0f} s", flush=True) json.dump(rows, open(out / f"{name}_events.json", "w"), indent=1) np.savez(out / f"{name}_partons.npz", **partons) np.savez(out / f"{name}_surface.npz", **cuts) if __name__ == "__main__": main(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])

The function run starts the script in a new Python process (sys.executable is this notebook's Python), sends everything it prints, with the modules' long log, into <name>.log, and reads back what it wrote. MUSIC prints the energy of its sources, the strings and the nucleon remnants, at the start of each event; we take it from the log, as a fingerprint of the initial state.

import json, re, subprocess, sys, time

def run(user_xml, name):
    """Run oo_events.py on a user XML in its own process -> one row per event."""
    t0 = time.time()
    with open(OUT / f"{name}.log", "w") as log:
        done = subprocess.run([sys.executable, OUT / "oo_events.py", user_xml, name],
                              stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
    text = (OUT / f"{name}.log").read_text(errors="replace")
    if done.returncode != 0:
        print(text[-3000:])
        raise RuntimeError(f"{name}: X-SCAPE failed, see {OUT / name}.log")
    table = pd.DataFrame(json.load(open(OUT / f"{name}_events.json"))).set_index("event")
    e_src = [float(v) for v in re.findall(r"\]\s+total energy = ([\d.]+) GeV", text)]
    table.insert(5, "E sources [GeV]", e_src)
    print(f"{name}: {len(table)} events in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s;",
          re.search(r"^modules: .*$", text, re.M).group(0))
    return table
