One row per collision:

  • pthat: the hard scattering's \(\hat p_T\) in GeV, within the 20–40 GeV window of the XML.
  • npart, ncoll, strings, b: the geometry. Of the 32 nucleons, npart took part in the collision; ncoll is the number of nucleon–nucleon collisions; strings the number of strings they made; \(b\) is in fm.
  • cells, tau_max: the freeze-out surface, as cells, and the proper time in fm/c at which the last of the fluid froze out. An O+O fireball lives about 4 fm/c.
  • final partons: what the energy loss handed to the jet hadronization.
  • bulk hadrons / oversample and jet hadrons: the two kinds of hadrons, in all directions.

The line above the table lists the modules in the order they run, by the names X-SCAPE gives them, with the modules each one holds in parentheses. The hard process holds the initial-state radiation (IsrManager) and the string maker (MCGlauberGenString), because the strings are made from what the hard pair leaves. The energy-loss manager holds JetEnergyLoss, which runs Matter and LBT. Their log is in out/02_first_events/oo_base.log.

Two showers carry the hard scattering: about 20 GeV of \(p_T\) each, as \(\hat p_T\) = 20.6 GeV says. The others start from softer partons that the hard process hands over as well; two of them fly along the beam, with large \(p_z\) and almost no \(p_T\). The medium kicked out a few recoils, with a few GeV of \(p_T\), and the holes record the smaller momentum those partons had before. In O+O at 200 GeV the medium is small and short-lived, so it changes a 20 GeV jet by a few GeV at most.

What to notice.

  • Each collision has its own \(dN/d\eta\). The heights differ by up to a factor 1.4, and the shapes are lumpy and asymmetric: the strings break the boost invariance along the beam, so an event can have more hadrons on one side. Smooth, symmetric distributions appear only after averaging over many events (tutorial 05). The 100 oversamples reduce the sampling noise, not these event-by-event fluctuations: they all come from the same fluid.
  • The bulk dominates at low \(p_T\), the jet at high \(p_T\). The bulk spectrum falls about exponentially, as for a thermal source moving with the flow. The jet hadrons fall much more slowly and take over above about 1 GeV. Below 1 GeV they are still about half as many as the bulk hadrons: iColoredHadronization strings the jet partons together with the remnants of the two colliding nucleons, and those strings make soft hadrons too. In a small system like O+O, the hard scattering is a sizable part of the whole event.

def eta_over_s(T, xml_path):
    """MUSIC's eta/s(T) for T_dependent_Shear_to_S_ratio 3, from the XML's settings."""
    m = ET.parse(xml_path).getroot().find("Hydro/MUSIC")
    f = lambda tag: float(m.findtext(tag))
    kink, Tk = f("shear_viscosity_3_at_kink"), f("shear_viscosity_3_T_kink_in_GeV")
    slope = np.where(T < Tk, f("shear_viscosity_3_low_T_slope_in_GeV"),
                     f("shear_viscosity_3_high_T_slope_in_GeV"))
    return np.maximum(kink + slope * (T - Tk), 1e-3)

What should change? Right after the collision the fluid expands fastest along the beam. Shear viscosity resists this anisotropic expansion: it lowers the pressure along the beam and raises it in the transverse plane. More viscous fluid therefore pushes outward harder, builds up more radial flow, and its hadrons come out with larger \(p_T\). Viscosity also produces entropy, so a little more multiplicity is expected.

The fluid's edge stays near \(|x| \approx 3.3\) fm until \(\tau \approx 3\) fm/c, then the cold region eats its way in, and the middle freezes out last, at \(\tau \approx 4.3\) fm/c. def bulk_pt(name):
    """The charged bulk pT spectrum at |eta| < 1, per event and oversample, of all events."""
    a = js.HadronArray.from_h5(OUT / f"{name}_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5").to_awkward(by_unit=True)

What to notice.

  • The mean \(p_T\) rises in each event, by 3–5 %, two to four times the error of the difference. The multiplicity rises too, but only by 1–3 %, within about one error per event.
  • The ratio of the spectra rises with \(p_T\). Below 0.5 GeV the two runs agree; above, the more viscous fluid gives more hadrons, up to about 25 % more near 1–1.5 GeV: a flatter, harder spectrum. This is the stronger radial flow of the surface, now in the hadrons. The viscous correction \(\delta f\) that iSS adds to the hadrons' momentum distribution grows with \(\eta/s\) too, and also shapes the spectrum. Above about 1.5 GeV the errors are large: there are few bulk hadrons there.

This is how \(\eta/s\) is constrained in practice: its effects on spectra and flow are compared over many events, with everything else fixed, and fitted to data. The famous signature is the elliptic flow \(v_2\), which viscosity damps. In central O+O collisions \(v_2\) comes from fluctuations and is small, so measuring it needs many more events than three.

docs.title: 02 · Your first events in Python¶
docs.text:
Time: 40 minutes · Needs: X-SCAPE (the production container, the Mac wheel or a source build) · Data: none: the notebook makes its own (about 10 MB in out/)

Tutorial 01 read files that someone else made. Here you make your own: three O+O collisions at 200 GeV, each with a hard scattering, run through the whole X-SCAPE chain from a Python loop with the Pythonic interface of PyJetscape. Along the way:

  • what each stage of the chain does, and what it hands to the next;
  • the hadrons it produces, as numpy and awkward arrays, with a first \(dN/d\eta\) and \(p_T\) spectrum;
  • one physics setting changed, the shear viscosity of the fluid, and its effect on the same three collisions.

The two runs take about a minute on a GPU (MUSIC on the CPU is several times slower).

Reference pages: Your first event, The Pythonic interface, The physics.

Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics. The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

The outputs shown were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal.

docs.title: 1. The chain of stages¶
docs.text:
An X-SCAPE run is a list of modules, one per stage of a collision, called in order for every event. Which modules run, and with which settings, is set by two XML files: the main XML (config/jetscape_main.xml), which holds a default for every setting, and the user XML, which names the modules of this run and changes what differs from the defaults. We start from the user XML of the example pythonic/oo_workflow.py (its page). It runs the physics settings of the O+O production.

From the first stage to the last:

  1. Initial state (3dMCGlauber). The nucleons of the two oxygen nuclei are placed in the transverse plane and collide where they overlap. Each nucleon–nucleon collision can stretch a QCD string between the two colliding partons; the strings carry the energy that will become the fluid. The impact parameter \(b\) sets the centrality.
  2. Hard scattering (PYTHIA 8). In one of the nucleon–nucleon collisions two partons scatter with a large momentum transfer, \(\hat p_T\). They will become jets. The incoming partons radiate before the scattering (initial-state radiation, iMATTER here), and the strings are made from what the hard pair left.
  3. Hydro (MUSIC). The strings deposit their energy and momentum into a fluid as they decelerate. MUSIC evolves it with viscous relativistic hydrodynamics: the quark–gluon plasma expands, cools and builds up flow. Its friction is set by the shear viscosity \(\eta/s\) and the bulk viscosity \(\zeta/s\), both functions of the temperature.
  4. Energy loss (Matter + LBT). The hard partons shower and scatter in the fluid as it evolves. MATTER handles the early, highly virtual stage of the shower, LBT the on-shell partons below the virtuality \(Q_0\). The medium kicks out recoil partons and leaves holes (partons of negative energy that carry what the medium lost).
  5. Freeze-out (MUSIC). Where the fluid cools below \(T_{fo}\) = 150 MeV it stops being a fluid. MUSIC records that boundary, a 3D hypersurface in space-time, as small cells with their flow velocity and viscous corrections.
  6. Hadrons. iSS turns the freeze-out surface into hadrons with the Cooper–Frye formula (the bulk), and decays the resonances. Since this is random sampling of one fluid, it can be repeated: each repetition is an oversample. The partons of the hard scattering are turned into hadrons along their colour lines by iColoredHadronization (the jet hadrons).

The settings behind each stage, read from the XML:

docs.title: 2. Run the events¶
docs.text:
Three pieces of the Pythonic interface run the chain:

  • js.JobDir(out, xml) gives the run a working directory of its own. MUSIC, 3dMCGlauber and iSS read input tables from the current directory and write side files there, and the XML has paths relative to the X-SCAPE build. JobDir copies the XML to out/, makes its paths absolute, links the tables, changes into out/work/<name> and back, and cleans up.
  • js.per_event(main_xml, user_xml) makes the driver. Entering the with block initializes every module (Init, ExecInit), leaving it finishes them.
  • driver.events() runs one event per step of the loop. Inside the loop the event's results are in memory: the modules are properties of the driver (driver.hydro, driver.energy_loss_manager, driver.soft_particlization, ...), and their ..._array() methods return numpy copies that stay valid after the event.

The hadrons go into two files in the format of all productions (HadronH5Writer): the bulk (one unit per event, one sample per oversample) and the jet hadrons (one sample per event). We also keep a few numbers of each event: its hard scattering, its Glauber geometry, its freeze-out surface and its final partons.

One run, one Python process. X-SCAPE reads its XML files once per process: a second per_event driver in the same process would still see the first run's settings. (It also numbers its modules over the whole process, and the numbers enter their random seeds.) So we write the event loop into a small script and run it in a process of its own for each XML, as the production scripts do. The next cell writes the script (%%writefile):

docs.title: The partons of the hard scattering¶
docs.text: final_parton_array() returns a numpy record array: one row per parton, with named fields shower, pid, pstat, E, px, py, pz, t, x, y, z, .... Each shower starts from one parton that the hard process handed over. js.to_awkward groups the partons by shower, as a jagged array of four-vectors, so \(p_T\), \(\eta\) and \(\phi\) are computed on demand. The status pstat marks what the medium did: \(1\) for a recoil, a parton kicked out of the medium, and \(-1\) for a hole. Holes are kept apart, so we sum over the others:

docs.title: The hadron files¶
docs.text: HadronArray.from_h5 reads a hadron file back: one array per field (pid, p, ...), grouped into samples, with the per-unit table that the writer received (info["units"]).

docs.title: Nested views with awkward¶
docs.text:
to_awkward() makes a nested view of the same arrays, with four-vector kinematics. by_unit=True nests the bulk as events × oversamples × hadrons.

js.select picks species, by their names in the particle package ("pi+", ["K+", "K-"], ["p", "p~"]) or by class ("charged", "meson", "baryon", "strange"). It returns a mask of the same nesting, so b[js.select(b, "charged")] keeps the charged hadrons of every oversample. For decayed hadrons, as here, "charged" picks exactly the stable charged hadrons (and leptons) of hadrons_h5.CHARGED, the list all the analysis tools use. ak.num and ak.sum count along an axis, and the mean over the oversamples of an event (axis=1) is that event's average:

docs.title: \(dN/d\eta\) and \(p_T\) spectra¶
docs.text: Now as histograms, with hist and Weight storage, which keeps the statistical errors. Each bulk hadron is weighted by \(1/N_\text{oversamples}\), so the yields are per oversample, that is per collision. The errors are the sampling errors of the oversamples only: the three collisions are three different events, not three measurements of one.

docs.title: 4. Change one setting: the shear viscosity¶
docs.text:
Now a physics question. How does the friction of the plasma, its shear viscosity, change what comes out? The relevant quantity is the ratio of the shear viscosity to the entropy density, \(\eta/s\). Strongly coupled theories suggest a lower bound near \(1/4\pi \approx 0.08\), and the QGP is thought to be close to it: it is the most nearly perfect fluid known.

In this XML, \(\eta/s\) depends on the temperature: it is smallest at a kink temperature \(T_k\) = 206 MeV and rises linearly on both sides,

\[\frac{\eta}{s}(T) = \left(\frac{\eta}{s}\right)_k + a_{\pm}\,(T - T_k),\]

with \(a_\pm = \pm 1.999\) GeV\(^{-1}\). We raise \((\eta/s)_k\) from 0.108 to 0.30, which shifts the whole curve up by 0.19, and change nothing else:

docs.title: Making the comparison fair¶
docs.text:
With three events, the differences between collisions (up to a factor 1.4 in multiplicity) are far larger than the effect we look for. So we compare the same three collisions, once with each value. We run the new XML with the same seed. The modules before the hydro then draw the same random numbers: the same nucleons, strings and hard scattering. MUSIC itself has no random numbers. Any difference in the fluid then comes from \(\eta/s\) alone.

This only works when the change keeps the list of modules. The modules take their random numbers from engines seeded from the one seed, in the order of the task list. A module added or removed can change what the others receive, and the events stop matching (exercise 2). We check that the inputs agree, event by event:

docs.title: The fluid¶
docs.text: The freeze-out surface needs no sampling, so its numbers carry no statistical error. The table compares its lifetime, its number of cells and the mean transverse flow on it, each cell weighted by the fluid that crosses it. The figure shows, on the left, a cut through event 0's surface at \(y \approx 0\), \(\eta_s \approx 0\), colored by the flow \(u^x\) (positive outward on the right, negative on the left), and on the right the distribution of the transverse flow \(u_T\) over the whole surface, for both runs:

docs.title: The hadrons¶
docs.text: The bulk hadrons are sampled, so their averages have errors. With 100 oversamples per event, the error of the mean \(p_T\) is about 1 %:

docs.title: 5. Without the notebook¶
docs.text:
The same run, as a script, is the example the notebook started from. In your copy of the examples (xscape-examples makes one; in a checkout it is contribs/PyJetscape/example/pythonic/):

python oo_workflow.py --xml <this folder>/out/02_first_events/oo_eta030.xml --outdir out_eta030
python oo_workflow.py --events 10 --seed 3 --outdir out_oo_s3

It writes the same two kinds of hadron files. And X-SCAPE runs a user XML without Python at all, with its own executable. On a Mac, the wheel's xscape-run copies both XMLs into a run directory, makes their paths absolute, links the tables and checks the XML before it starts:

xscape-run -w ~/xscape/runs/oo -u <this folder>/out/02_first_events/oo_base.xml

Then X-SCAPE's own writers decide what is stored, and this XML switches them all off: set, for example, <JetScapeWriterFinalStateHadronsAscii> on </JetScapeWriterFinalStateHadronsAscii> in a copy. In a source build the script behind xscape-run is X-SCAPE/examples/run_in_workdir.sh. Details: Your first event.

docs.title: Check your result¶
docs.text: Your numbers come from your own run of X-SCAPE. With the same build they are the ones shown, bit for bit. Another GPU, or MUSIC on the CPU, changes them slightly, and another build of PYTHIA or 3dMCGlauber can give other collisions altogether. The check allows for that: the comparison must be fair and show the same physics everywhere, and the numbers must match where the collisions do:

docs.title: Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. Another setting. Switch the bulk viscosity off (bulk_viscosity_3_max 0), or lower \((\eta/s)_k\) to 0.08, and compare with the first run the same way. Which way does the mean \(p_T\) move?
  2. Removing a module. Delete the <Lbt> element from a copy of oo_base.xml (so that only MATTER acts on the jets) and run it. Compare the inputs table with the first run: which events are still the same collisions? How would you switch LBT off and keep the events? (Look at <in_vac> in the XML.)
  3. The jets. In oo_base_partons.npz and oo_eta030_partons.npz, compare the recoils and holes of each event. Does the jet lose more energy in the more viscous fluid? Think about which medium property the energy loss reads (temperature, flow) before you look.
  4. More events. Run 10 events with each \(\eta/s\) (edit nEvents, or use oo_workflow.py) and compare the mean \(p_T\) averaged over events, with the event-to-event spread as its error.

OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

SHORT = [(str(JOB), "out/03_production/AuAu"), (str(OUT), "out/03_production"),
         (str(PROD), "<prod>"), (str(EX), "<examples>"), (str(paths.build_dir()), "<build>"),
         (str(paths.xscape_root()), "<X-SCAPE>")]

def tidy(text):
    """This machine's paths -> short names."""
    for long, short in SHORT:
        text = text.replace(long, short)
    return text

def script(name, *args, log=None):
    """Run a script of the production folder in a new process -> (its output, seconds).
    The full output also goes to the file `log`, if given."""
    t0 = time.time()
    done = subprocess.run([sys.executable, PROD / name, *map(str, args)], cwd=OUT, text=True,
                          stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
    if log:
        Path(log).write_text(done.stdout)
    if done.returncode != 0:
        print(tidy(done.stdout[-3000:]))
        raise RuntimeError(f"{name} failed")
    return tidy(done.stdout), time.time() - t0

The first line is the plan: 2 events with seed 101, PYTHIA with \(\hat p_T\) 30–40 GeV and the leading parton at \(|y| < 0.6\), one background for both jets (reuse 2), the jet's energy deposited in the fluid, and both freeze-out surfaces stored for hadronization. The output grid is the one the hydro history is stored on (tutorial 06). What did the driver change in the template? We compare the two XMLs element by element:

import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

def leaves(el, path=""):
    """{path: text} of every element without children."""
    out = {}
    for child in el:
        if not isinstance(child.tag, str):
            continue                                  # a comment
        p = f"{path}/{child.tag}"
        while p in out:
            p += "+"                                  # a repeated tag
        out.update(leaves(child, p) if len(child) else {p: (child.text or "").strip()})
    return out

changed = [(k, template.get(k, "(absent)"), job_xml.get(k, "(absent)"))
           for k in sorted(set(template) | set(job_xml)) if template.get(k) != job_xml.get(k)]

What to notice. Only the job changed: the number of events, the seed, the window and the parton cut of PYTHIA, the reuse of the background, and the freeze-out surface that the particlize file needs. Two technical switches come with them: slim_bulk_info (a smaller copy of the medium for the energy loss, with the same output) and the extra hard scatterings, off. Every physics setting is the template's. This is what makes the jobs of a campaign, and campaigns made months apart, comparable: each records its full XML, and you can check that the physics agrees (tutorial 04, section 7).

Per event, the pair writer reports how many time frames each hydro leg has, how many droplets the jets deposited and how much energy they carried, and how many leading frames of the two legs are identical (before the first droplet arrives). The particlize writer reports the cells of each leg's freeze-out surface. The background (bg) is the same for both events: it was computed once.

What to notice.

  • One background unit for two events. bulk_bg has a single unit: the background both jets shared. A jet event is bulk_jet + jet_frag; its background is bulk_bg's unit bg_unit of the particlize file.
  • The common seeds. Both bulk_jet units carry the seed of their background unit: that is --common-seeds. The jet fragments have their own seed per event.
  • About 8,400 hadrons per bulk sample (all species, all rapidities: one central Au+Au collision), and a few tens per fragmentation of the jets.
  • source_uuid ties each hadron file to its particlize file; the readers refuse mismatched files (tutorial 04).

The two estimates of the same quantity differ by a factor 1.6: a single job's \(\sigma\) is noisy. A campaign combines the estimates of all its jobs. The data set auau_stats is a small campaign: 4 jobs of 30 events, three windows 10–20, 20–30 and 30–50 GeV, 2 jets per window per background. Each job recorded its own estimates, and the campaign file of run_h5toROOT.py holds the combination:

What to notice.

  • The cross section falls by three orders of magnitude from the 10–20 to the 30–50 GeV window, yet each window has 40 events. Generated over 10–50 GeV in one go, only about one event in a thousand would land in the 30–50 GeV window.
  • The jobs' estimates scatter by up to about 30 % around the combined value: each job saw only 12–24 PYTHIA events per window. The combined value carries an error of 11–13 %.
  • weight_mb = \(\sigma\) / n_events is the weight of one event of that window. A spectrum over all windows is the sum of the windows' histograms, each event weighted by its window's weight_mb (tutorial 05). Results for one window alone need no weights.

A dry run shows the plan of one such job. We give it --seed 0 and a campaign name, as a campaign would: the seed is drawn from the operating system (yours will differ), the file is named by campaign and job number, and a dry run records nothing in the registry:

oversample_bg: per-pthat-bin gives each background \(M \times\) oversample samples, as many as the \(M\) jet events of one window have together: the right balance for results per window. Correlated sampling (--correlated) works in the job as in stage 2; auau_stats did not use it, our job and auau_pair_mini did. Use it when the analysis is jet minus background, and analyse such files sample by sample (tutorial 07).

Decide the hadron settings once per campaign. The number of oversamples, the correlation, the precision (--keep-bits-p/-x) and the selection (--eta-max, --charged, --no-x) must be the same for every job: restarts skip complete files whatever settings made them.

pair_mini() {
  local D="$OUT/AuAu_pair_mini"
  log "AuAu_pair_mini -> $D"

   $PY run_prod_jet.py --events 5 --reuse 5 --seed 101 --pthat-min 30 --pthat-max 40 \
       --parton-ymax 0.6 --write-particlize both --outdir "$D" &&
   $PY hadronize.py "$D/AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101_particlize.h5" \
       --correlated --common-seeds --oversample 200 --n-frag 20 &&
   $PY run_h5toROOT.py "$D" --writer uproot)
} 

stats() {
  local D="$OUT/AuAu_stats"
  log "AuAu_stats -> $D"
  (cd "$EX/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet" &&
   printf '%s\n' 201 202 203 204 | xargs -P "$JOBS" -I{} \
     $PY run_prod_jet.py --events 30 --seed {} --campaign stats \
       --pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-50 --jets-per-bin 2 --parton-ymax 0.6 \
       --hadrons-only --oversample 10 --n-frag 10 --no-x --outdir "$D" &&
   mkdir -p "$OUT/AuAu_stats_primaries" &&       # the undecayed hadrons (for an afterburner):
   mv "$D"/*_primary.h5 "$OUT/AuAu_stats_primaries/" &&   # not part of the set
   $PY run_h5toROOT.py "$D" --writer uproot -j "$JOBS")
}

Read them with this tutorial in mind.

  • pair_mini is our job with five jets: run_prod_jet.py --events 5 --reuse 5 --seed 101 ..., then hadronize.py --correlated --common-seeds --oversample 200 --n-frag 20 and run_h5toROOT.py --writer uproot. Its first two events are ours (section 4).
  • stats is a campaign of four jobs with seeds 201–204, three windows and two jets per window per background, hadrons made in the job (--hadrons-only, 10 oversamples, no positions), started three at a time by xargs -P instead of run_jobs.sh. It moves the undecayed hadrons (*_primary.h5, kept for a later hadronic afterburner) out of the set, then writes the ROOT files and the campaign file.
  • Fixed seeds make every set reproducible with the same build. The script's header states the machine and environment, and that uploaded sets are never overwritten.
  • The last function, upload, sends each set with js_osdf.py upload --what all --prefix tutorials/v2.

docs.title: 03 · The production scripts¶
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes · Needs: X-SCAPE (the production container, the Mac wheel or a source build) · Data: auau_stats and auau_pair_mini: a few job records (kB) and one table; the notebook makes its own job (about 0.7 GB in out/)

Tutorial 02 ran events from a Python loop. For physics you need thousands of events, made the same way, recorded so that they can be checked, combined and shared. That is what the production scripts do. This tutorial runs one real production job, a central Au+Au collision with two jets, through both stages, and looks at every file each step writes:

  • the driver run_prod_jet.py, its user XML and its options;
  • seeds, and why a seed is a set of collisions;
  • stage 2: hadronization with hadronize.py, and the ROOT conversion;
  • \(\hat p_T\) windows and their cross sections, hadrons made in the job, correlated sampling;
  • how many jobs make a campaign, how it is watched, and how its files are shared on the OSDF.

The job is a small copy of the one behind the data set auau_pair_mini of tutorials 04, 06 and 07, and the last section shows the recipe of all the tutorial data.

Reference pages: Running the productions, Au+Au jets, Clusters, GPUs and monitoring, Data on the OSDF.

Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics. The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

The outputs shown were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal.

docs.title: 1. Jobs and campaigns¶
docs.text:
A production is a folder of ready-made scripts for one physics setup. Its driver runs one job: one seed, N events, one set of output files. A campaign is many jobs of the same setup, each with its own seed, run side by side on one or many GPUs. Every production works this way:

production physics driver prod_AuAu_0_10 0–10 % Au+Au at 200 GeV, hydro only run_prod.py prod_AuAu_0_10_jet the same medium with a jet, whose lost energy flows back into a second hydro run run_prod_jet.py prod_OO_isr O+O at 200 GeV with initial-state radiation (tutorial 02's chain) run_prod_oo_isr.py

We use the main production, prod_AuAu_0_10_jet. Its folder holds the driver, the stage-2 scripts and run_jobs.sh for campaigns. In the container and the Mac wheel the scripts sit in a read-only place, which is fine: they write only into the output directory we give them. The helper script runs one of them with this notebook's Python, in a process of its own, and shortens the paths in what it prints:

docs.title: 2. The user XML and the job XML¶
docs.text:
The physics is in a user XML, as in tutorial 02. The production's template is config/AuAu_MCGlauber_MUSIC_0_10_jet.xml: the initial state, the hydro with its viscosities, Matter and LBT, the liquefier that turns the jet's lost energy into sources for the fluid. The driver takes it, or your own with --user-xml my.xml, and fills in what belongs to the job: the number of events, the seed, the hard process and its window, what to store. It checks the result and writes it next to the output, as <stem>.xml; the same text goes into the files (tutorial 04).

So, to change the physics, copy the template, edit the copy and pass it with --user-xml; to change the job, use the options. A dry run (--dry-run) checks everything, writes the job XML and prints the plan, without running an event. Here is our job, a small copy of the one behind auau_pair_mini:

docs.title: 3. Seeds¶
docs.text:
--seed S sets X-SCAPE's <Random><seed>. Every random number of the job derives from it: the nucleons and strings of the initial state, PYTHIA's hard scattering, the energy loss. So a seed is a set of collisions: the same seed, XML and build give the same events, bit for bit. That is what you want to compare two settings on the same collisions (tutorial 02 did this with \(\eta/s\)), and exactly what you must avoid in a campaign meant to add statistics.

  • An explicit seed (--seed 101) names the file (..._seed0101.h5) and reproduces it.
  • --seed 0 draws a new seed from the operating system's entropy, one that the seed registry has not seen, and records it in the files and the job record, so the job stays reproducible. The file is then named by the campaign and a job number (AuAu_0_10_jet_<campaign>_0001.h5). This is what campaigns use.
  • Not X-SCAPE's own seed 0. In a plain X-SCAPE XML, seed 0 means "take the clock": PYTHIA then seeds itself from the time in seconds, so jobs started together get the same jets, and the seed is recorded nowhere. The drivers never pass 0 to X-SCAPE.
  • The seed registry is seeds_used.tsv in the parent of the output directory: every job appends its seed, under a lock, and a seed used before is reported. Campaigns kept side by side in one directory share it. Our job writes to out/03_production/AuAu, so its registry is out/03_production/seeds_used.tsv.

docs.title: 4. Stage 1: hydro and jets¶
docs.text: Now the job itself. The background (MUSIC_1) runs once; each of the two jets showers in it with Matter and LBT; the energy and momentum the jet loses becomes droplets, sources for a second hydro run with the same strings (MUSIC_2). One Au+Au jet event takes about 10–15 s on an Apple Silicon GPU, so the job takes well under a minute. Like run_jobs.sh, we keep the driver's output as <stem>.log in the output directory:

docs.title: A seed is a set of collisions¶
docs.text: The data set auau_pair_mini of tutorials 04, 06 and 07 was made with the same template, the same window and seed 101, but five jets per background (--reuse 5). A background is made once per reuse events, so its first two events should be ours (with the build the data were made with). The pair files record each event's \(\hat p_T\) and droplets (diag/):

docs.title: 5. Stage 2: hadrons¶
docs.text:
hadronize.py turns one particlize file into hadrons, on the CPU, without MUSIC: iSS samples each stored freeze-out surface (the bulk), and PYTHIA fragments the stored final partons (the jet fragments). Since the surfaces are stored, stage 2 can be repeated any number of times, with more oversamples or other settings, without the expensive stage 1. The options we use:

  • --oversample 20: iSS samples per surface. Productions use 100–500; we keep it small.
  • --n-frag 5: PYTHIA fragmentations of each event's partons.
  • --correlated --common-seeds: correlated sampling. Sample \(k\) of a jet event and sample \(k\) of its background use the same random numbers, addressed by the surface cell. Where the two surfaces agree, they give the same hadrons, so jet minus background, the jet's wake in hadrons, is far less noisy (tutorial 07).

Each unit (an event, or a background) gets its own seed, derived from the base seed (--seed, default 1), the particlize file's unique id, the tag and the unit, and recorded in the file. For a whole campaign, run_hadronize.py runs hadronize.py over a directory, several files at once, and skips files whose hadrons are complete.

docs.title: ROOT files¶
docs.text: run_h5toROOT.py converts a directory of hadronized jobs into ROOT files, one per job (RNTuple), plus a campaign file with the cross sections of all jobs together. It needs no ROOT installation with --writer uproot. Tutorials 09 and 10 work with these files.

docs.title: 6. The job, step by step: what we have now¶
docs.text:
step command writes needs stage 1 run_prod_jet.py ... --write-particlize both <stem>.h5, <stem>_particlize.h5, .json, .xml a GPU (or a slow CPU) stage 2 hadronize.py <stem>_particlize.h5 (or run_hadronize.py DIR) <stem>_hadrons_{bulk_jet,bulk_bg,jet_frag}.h5 CPUs ROOT run_h5toROOT.py DIR <stem>_hadrons.root, <campaign>_campaign.root CPUs

The particlize file is self-contained: it can travel to another cluster for stage 2 without the pair file. Our files, all together:

docs.title: 7. \(\hat p_T\) windows and cross sections¶
docs.text:
The jet cross section falls steeply with \(p_T\). A sample generated over one wide \(\hat p_T\) range would be almost all low-\(\hat p_T\) events. So the productions generate in windows of \(\hat p_T\) and weight each window by its cross section afterwards.

  • --pthat-min/--pthat-max set one window (our job: 30–40 GeV).
  • --pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-50 runs K windows in one job, one PYTHIA per window with its own seed and cross section; event \(i\) uses window \(i \bmod K\).
  • --jets-per-bin M gives every background M jets in each window: reuse becomes \(K \times M\), and the events per job must be a multiple of it. A background costs about as much as a jet leg, so sharing it saves nearly half the time.

PYTHIA estimates each window's cross section \(\sigma\) from the events it generates. With the parton cut (--parton-ymax) rejected events are regenerated, and \(\sigma\) is multiplied by the accepted fraction. Our job tried only 2 events, so its \(\sigma\) is a rough estimate; auau_pair_mini tried 6 for the same window:

docs.title: 8. Hadrons in the job, and correlated sampling¶
docs.text: That dry run also used --hadrons-only: iSS and the jet fragmentation run inside the GPU job, exactly as hadronize.py would (same code, settings and seeds), and the job writes only the hadron files and its record: no pair file, no particlize file, no stage 2. It suits campaigns with little oversampling, here 10 samples per jet event. The price: no surfaces, so no new samples later, and no hydro history. Measured on the GB10 (the Au+Au jets page), it wrote 0.64 MB per event, against about 160 MB in two stages. auau_stats was made this way; its job record keeps the hadronization settings:

docs.title: 9. From a job to a campaign¶
docs.text:
Nothing below runs in this notebook; each is a command for a terminal.

run_jobs.sh runs many jobs of one production, -j P at a time on one GPU, each in its own working directory:

cd <your copy of the examples>/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet
./run_jobs.sh [-j P] [--mps] [--stagger S] [--campaign NAME] NJOBS EVENTS_PER_JOB FIRST_SEED [OUTDIR] [driver options]

# 67 jobs x 15 events, new seeds, three windows, 5 jets per window per background
./run_jobs.sh -j 3 --campaign pth10-40_c1 67 15 0 ~/xscape/prod/AuAu_c1 \
    --pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-40 --jets-per-bin 5 --parton-ymax 0.6 --write-particlize both
  • FIRST_SEED 0 gives every job a new seed through --seed 0 (a campaign); FIRST_SEED 1 gives seeds 1, 2, ... (to reproduce files, or to compare settings on the same collisions).
  • OUTDIR is the argument after FIRST_SEED; one campaign per OUTDIR. Every job leaves <stem>.log, .json, .xml there, and the campaign ends with run_jobs.finished.
  • Restart with the same command: jobs whose .json says complete are skipped, the others are redone.
  • On a Mac, split the cores between the jobs: OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive ./run_jobs.sh -j 3 ... on a 16-core M3 Max. On CUDA, --mps lets the jobs share the GPU.

utils/prodwizard.py plans a campaign before it runs: pick a preset (auau_jet, auau_hadrons_only, oo_hadrons, ...) and a machine (mac_wheel, 2x3090, slurm_a100, ...), and it writes the launch command with the measured settings for that machine and estimates events per hour, duration, disk and memory. It checks the plan (events per job a multiple of windows × jets, memory, disk) and never starts jobs:

utils/prodwizard.py --preset auau_jet --machine mac_wheel --events 300     # xscape-prodwizard in the wheel

utils/jobmon.py watches a running or finished campaign from what the jobs write (logs, job records): jobs done, running and failed, events per hour, the time left, disk per event, and checks such as the deposition check, which flags the rare job whose jets deposited far less energy than the rest:

utils/jobmon.py ~/xscape/prod/AuAu_c1 --watch      # xscape-jobmon in the wheel

On a cluster with SLURM, utils/slurm_prod_array.sh runs a campaign as a job array in the production container: each array task gets one GPU and runs P jobs on it, all tasks sharing one seed registry. A GPU needs several jobs at once to stay busy, so one SLURM job per production job would waste it. Stage 2 runs on CPU nodes with utils/slurm_hadronize.sh:

SIF=$PWD/xscape_prod.sif CAMPAIGN=pth10-40_c2 NJOBS=40 EVENTS=15 \
  EXTRA_ARGS="--pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-40 --jets-per-bin 5 --parton-ymax 0.6 --write-particlize both" \
  sbatch --array=0-19 utils/slurm_prod_array.sh

The sizes per GPU type, the launch settings and a 12,000-event example are on Clusters, GPUs and monitoring.

docs.title: 10. Sharing the files on the OSDF¶
docs.text:
The tutorial data come from the OSDF (Open Science Data Federation), a network of data origins and caches. Reading is public: with pelicanfs in Python (osdf:// URLs, tutorial 01), or over plain HTTPS. Writing to the namespace osdf:///fno4hic needs a login. utils/remote_transfer/js_osdf.py (xscape-osdf in the Mac wheel) moves whole productions or kinds of files:

./js_osdf.py login                                         # once: a link to log in from any browser
./js_osdf.py upload ~/xscape/prod/AuAu_c1 --what h5 --dry-run     # what would go
./js_osdf.py upload ~/xscape/prod/AuAu_c1 --what h5        # -> osdf:///fno4hic/AuAu_c1/
./js_osdf.py download AuAu_c1 --what root --to /scratch    # anyone, no login
  • --what picks files by kind: h5 (particlize and hadron files: everything an analysis needs), root, pair (the hydro, for the ML hydro), all.
  • Incomplete files (an HDF5 file whose complete attribute is false, *.part) are left out. Each upload is checked: the size at the origin, and a CRC32C recorded in a manifest in the remote folder, which downloads (and get_data.py) check against.
  • Whatever is uploaded can be read by everyone.
  • Uploaded files are never overwritten. The OSDF caches keep a copy of a file for a long time, so a file replaced at the origin can still be served in its old version, and readers would get different data under one name. A changed data set is a new version under a new name instead: the tutorial data live under tutorials/v2/, and a change would become v3.

This notebook uploads nothing.

docs.title: 11. A worked example: how the tutorial data were made¶
docs.text: The data sets of the tutorials were made by one script, data_recipes/make_v2.sh in this folder: each set is a function of a few production commands. Here are the two Au+Au sets:

docs.title: Check your result¶
docs.text: Your job ran on your setup. Its collisions are fixed by the seed and the build: another GPU or MUSIC on the CPU changes the numbers slightly, another build of PYTHIA or 3dMCGlauber can give other collisions. The hadrons of stage 2 also depend on the particlize file's unique id, so they change with every run of stage 1. The check allows for both:

docs.title: Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. The null test. Run one event with --no-deposit (and its own seed and output directory): MUSIC_2 then runs without the droplets, and the two legs must be identical. Check diag/frames_identical against diag/ntau_jet in the pair file. Why is this the first thing to run on a new machine or build?
  2. Stage 2 again. Run hadronize.py on our particlize file once more, with --tags jet_frag --seed 2 --force. Which hadron file changes, and which seeds? Then without --force: what happens?
  3. A campaign's arithmetic. With --dry-run, try --events 20 --pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-40 --jets-per-bin 5. What does the driver say, and why? Which numbers of events work?
  4. Plan a campaign. Run utils/prodwizard.py --list, then a plan for 300 Au+Au events on your machine (--preset auau_jet --machine mac_wheel --events 300, or a cluster). How long would it take, and how much disk would it need?

In order: the initial state is a 3D MC-Glauber model with strings (0–10 % central Au+Au). The hard scattering comes from PYTHIA. The fluid is MUSIC with temperature-dependent shear and bulk viscosities, which ends where the temperature falls below 150 MeV. The jet loses energy with MATTER at high virtuality and LBT below \(Q_0 = 2\) GeV. The CausalLiquefier turns the energy and momentum the jet loses into droplets that the fluid absorbs after a delay. Each step is explained in The physics.

What to notice.

  • E_droplets: the energy the jet handed to the fluid, from 16 to 54 GeV. The two hard partons together carry about \(2\hat p_T \approx\) 60–70 GeV, so in 0–10 % central Au+Au a large part of the jets' energy ends up in the medium. How much depends on the path through the fireball.
  • tau_identical: the two legs stay bit-identical until the first droplet arrives, about 1.1–1.4 fm/c. That is the jet's start (\(\tau = 0.5\) fm/c) plus the liquefier's delay.
  • tau_fo_jet vs tau_fo_bg: the jet leg freezes out later, by up to 2.8 fm/c. The deposited energy reheats the fluid, so its last part takes longer to cool to 150 MeV. This is why arr - arr_bg is only a "wake" while both legs still exist.

What to notice.

  • Almost every cell sits at \(T = T_\text{fo} = 0.15\) GeV: the surface is where the fluid cools through the freeze-out temperature.
  • About 1 % of the cells are colder, all at the very start of the hydro (\(\tau \approx 0.46\) fm/c). They are fluid that was already below 150 MeV when the hydro began, at the dilute edges of the fireball (large radius or large \(|\eta_s|\)). MUSIC freezes them out at once (Do_FreezeOut_lowtemp in the XML), so their energy is not lost.
  • The jet leg has about 1 % more cells than the background, from the reheated, slightly larger fluid. A leg with very different numbers would point to a broken hydro run.

import yaml

    """The settings that must agree between files you combine."""

        "output grid x": grid["x"],
        "EoS": A["eos_kind"],

docs.title: 04 · The files and their provenance¶
docs.text:
Time: 30 minutes · Needs: any setup · Data: auau_pair_mini (streamed: a few MB are read)

A production job writes several files, each for a different use. This tutorial opens every file of one job: a Au+Au collision with five jets. Along the way it shows what each stage of the simulation leaves behind, and where the job records how it was made: the seed, the physics settings, the software and the grid. Those records let you check that files belong together before you combine them.

Reference pages: What a production writes and The physics.

Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics. The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

The outputs shown were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal.

docs.title: 1. One job, its files¶
docs.text:
A jet production runs in two stages:

  1. Stage 1, on the GPU (run_prod_jet.py): the initial state, the hard scattering, the hydro of the background (MUSIC_1), the jet's energy loss in it (Matter + LBT), and the hydro again with the energy the jet deposited (MUSIC_2). It writes the pair file (both hydro evolutions), the particlize file (both freeze-out surfaces and the final partons), and the job record (.json, .xml).
  2. Stage 2, on the CPU (hadronize.py): Cooper–Frye sampling of each freeze-out surface and hadronization of the jet partons. It writes the hadron files: bulk_jet (the medium with the jet's wake), bulk_bg (the medium alone) and jet_frag (the jet's own hadrons). run_h5toROOT.py then copies them into a ROOT file.

Stage 2 can be repeated any number of times from the particlize file, with more oversamples or other settings, without rerunning the hydro.

All files of a job share its stem. The files of this set:

docs.title: 2. The job record¶
docs.text: <stem>.json summarises the job: its seed, what was simulated, how many events were written, and the cross section of the p̂T window.

docs.title: 3. The pair file: two hydro evolutions¶
docs.text:
<stem>.h5 holds the energy density and flow velocity of both hydro runs on a fixed grid in \((x, y, \eta_s, \tau)\): arr is the jet leg (MUSIC_2), arr_bg the background (MUSIC_1). Both start from the same initial condition, so arr - arr_bg is exactly what the jet did to the fluid. Tutorial 06 looks at that difference. Here we look at the layout and the per-event diagnostics.

The file is streamed: opening it and reading the diagnostics fetches a few MB of its 836 MB.

docs.title: 4. The particlize file: the input of hadronization¶
docs.text:
<stem>_particlize.h5 holds what stage 2 needs:

  • the freeze-out surface of each leg: a list of hypersurface cells with their position, normal vector \(d\Sigma_\mu\), flow \(u^\mu\), temperature and viscous corrections (32 columns per cell)
  • the final partons of the jet
  • the shower initiators: the partons that started the jet showers

The background's surface is stored once, and every event points to it through events/bg_unit.

docs.title: 5. The hadron files¶
docs.text:
Each hadron file holds one tag. The hadrons are in one flat table; the offsets mark the units (an event, or for bulk_bg a background) and their samples (Cooper–Frye oversamples or fragmentations):

tag from unit samples per unit here bulk_jet the jet leg's surface event 100 bulk_bg the background's surface background 500 = 100 × the 5 events using it jet_frag the final partons event 20

Each hadron file records the file_uuid of the particlize file it came from, as its source_uuid. The readers refuse a hadron file that does not match, which catches files renamed or mixed up between runs.

docs.title: 6. The ROOT file¶
docs.text: run_h5toROOT.py puts the three hadron tags and the event information into one ROOT file per job (RNTuple), plus a campaign file with the cross sections. uproot reads it without ROOT, also straight from the OSDF:

docs.title: 7. Before combining files: the settings¶
docs.text: Files can look alike and still differ in how they were made. Before you combine files from different jobs or campaigns, compare their settings. All of them are recorded in the attributes of the pair and particlize files:

docs.title: Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. Which jet lost the most energy? Event 0 deposited 54 GeV. Look at its partons' \(p_T\) and rapidity in diag (parton_pt_lead, parton_y_lead, ...). Is there a simple reason? (Tutorial 06 shows its path through the medium.)
  2. Another job. Compare production_settings with the older example event in the set auau_jet_event (file AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0003.h5). Which settings differ? Could the two be combined in one analysis?
  3. The surface. Histogram the \(\tau\) of event 0's surface cells (tau above) for the jet leg, and the same for the background (surface/bg). Where do the extra cells of the jet leg come from?

  • The wake in hadrons, from the hadron files: tutorial 07.

from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import CHARGED          # the |pid| of the charged hadrons

def mid_charged(ev, info):
    """A mask for the reader: charged hadrons at |eta| < 1."""
    return ev.charged & (np.abs(ev.eta) < 1)

per_sample = []
for k in range(r.n_oversamples(0)):
    s = r.jet_event(0, k, fragments=False)      # oversample k of bulk_jet alone
    p = np.asarray(s["p"], dtype=np.float64)
    eta = np.arcsinh(p[:, 3] / np.hypot(p[:, 1], p[:, 2]))
    per_sample.append(int(np.sum(np.isin(np.abs(s["pid"]), CHARGED) & (np.abs(eta) < 1))))
per_sample = np.array(per_sample)
n0, e0 = r.total("bulk_jet", mask=mid_charged, events=[0])
print("charged hadrons at |eta| < 1, per oversample:", per_sample.tolist())

      f"error of the mean {per_sample.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(per_sample)):.1f}")

by hand: mean 1479.6, spread 54.7, error of the mean 17.3
r.total(events=[0]): 1479.6 +- 12.2

HadronFileReader does exactly this for every event: it averages the samples of the event's unit, and then averages these per-event means over the events. Each event weighs the same, whatever its number of oversamples. Pooling all samples of a campaign instead would weigh each event by its number of oversamples: an event hadronized with 100 oversamples would count ten times as much as one with 10.

The error the reader returns is the sampling error of these means. It is computed as if every hadron were emitted independently (compound-Poisson), which gives 12 here. The ten oversamples scatter more than that: their spread of 55 gives an error of the mean of 17. Part of the difference is physics: a resonance decays into several hadrons at once, so the counts fluctuate more than Poisson (the Hadrons page quotes about 20 % for soft multiplicities). Part is chance: ten samples fix their own spread only to about ±25 %.

A shared background. The six events of a background share its bulk_bg unit. The reader counts that unit once for each event that uses it, so that the background and the jet events are averaged over the same collisions. The six copies are the same hadrons, so their errors add linearly, not in quadrature. That is why the background's error is larger here, although it has twice the oversamples:

error ratio 1.73; expected sqrt(6 events per background / 2x the oversamples) = 1.73

the 20 backgrounds: 1140 .. 1670, spread 169 -> error of the mean over collisions 37.8

Which error. The reader's error says how well the hadrons of these 120 events are known: it shrinks with more oversamples. The backgrounds themselves differ from collision to collision (the nuclei's positions, the impact parameter within 0–10 %), by much more than the sampling noise. For the mean over all central collisions, that spread is the error that counts, and only more collisions reduce it. With 20 backgrounds it is about 20 times the sampling error. Keep the two apart: oversamples make each event precise; only events make the campaign representative.

import hist

What to notice.

  • About 710 charged hadrons per unit of \(\eta\) at midrapidity, falling off towards \(|\eta| \approx 5\): the plateau and the shoulders of a central Au+Au collision at 200 GeV.
  • The jet adds very little: about 17 charged hadrons at \(|\eta| < 1\), of which about 8 are the jet's own fragments. The rest is the jet's wake in the fluid, which tutorial 07 measures precisely with correlated sampling. Here the legs were sampled independently, so the difference has a large error (±2 on 1,400), and single bins scatter by several hadrons.
  • The jet's hadrons are centred at midrapidity but spread over several units of \(\eta\), though the leading parton was at \(|y| < 0.6\): the other parton of the pair can sit at larger rapidity, and soft fragments spread out.

SPECIES = {"pi": r"$\pi^\pm$", "K": r"$K^\pm$", "p+pbar": r"$p, \bar p$"}
spectra = {}
for sp in SPECIES:
    sel = lambda ev, info, sp=sp: ev.species(sp) & (np.abs(ev.y) < 0.5)
    b = to_hist(*r.hist("bulk_bg", "pt", pt_edges, mask=sel, per_event=False), pt_edges, "pt", r"$p_T$ [GeV]")

    f = to_hist(*r.hist("jet_frag", "pt", pt_edges, mask=sel, per_event=False), pt_edges, "pt", r"$p_T$ [GeV]")
    spectra[sp] = {"bg": b, "jet": j + f, "frag": f}

What to notice.

  • Mass ordering. The heavier the hadron, the flatter its spectrum and the larger its \(\langle p_T \rangle\): pions about 0.5 GeV, kaons about 0.7, protons about 1.0. All three freeze out from the same fluid at the same temperature; the collective flow gives every hadron the same velocity boost, and a common velocity means more momentum for a heavier hadron.
  • The background ends at a few GeV. A thermal source at 150 MeV, even with strong flow, makes very few hadrons above 3 GeV: in these 120 events the background's spectra end at 4–5 GeV.
  • Above that, the jet events are all jet. The ratio jet events / background is close to 1 below 2 GeV and grows steeply above: at 3–4 GeV the jet events have several times the background's pions. The fragments of the jet stick out of the thermal spectrum, which is why high-\(p_T\) hadrons are a clean probe of the jet. Protons rise last: the bulk makes many protons at 2–3 GeV (flow pushes them there), while the jet's fragmentation makes few.

What to notice.

  • No bad runs. The cell ratios stay within a few per cent of 1, and every job's droplets per event are close to the median. A failed leg (ratio ≈ 3) or a job with almost no deposition would stand out at once.
  • The deposited energy varies far more from jet to jet than with p̂T. At the same p̂T it ranges over a factor of ten; the window means grow only slowly with p̂T. How much a jet gives to the fluid depends on the path of its partons through the fireball and on how long they stay in it. It can even exceed \(2\hat p_T\): p̂T is the transverse momentum, while the partons' energy also counts their longitudinal momentum, and the event's other partons from PYTHIA (initial-state radiation, multiple parton interactions) lose energy too.

The cross section includes the cut on the partons' rapidity: PYTHIA's estimate times the fraction of generated scatterings that passed it (the acceptance). Combining windows. For each window, the reader gives the per-event average \(\langle h\rangle_k\) of a histogram. A p̂T-inclusive result is the cross-section-weighted sum

\[\frac{d\sigma}{dp_T} = \sum_k \sigma_k\,\langle h \rangle_k ,\]

in mb/GeV, or divided by \(\sum_k \sigma_k\), the per-event average of a sample with the natural p̂T distribution (above 10 GeV). Each window's per-event mean already removes its own number of events, so the windows can have different event counts.

What to notice.

  • Each window covers its own range of hadron \(p_T\), and the windows overlap. The lowest window dominates the sum up to 6–8 GeV, the middle one around 10 GeV, and the highest one above 15 GeV.
  • A single hadron can make a spike. In the lowest window one hadron of 40 events × 10 fragmentations weighs \(\sigma_0/400\), more than the whole of the upper windows in that bin. The 12–15 GeV bin holds exactly one such hadron (printed above), and the sum jumps there. Where a window runs out of statistics, its last few hadrons give spikes like this. The cure is more events in that window, or windows whose ranges match the \(p_T\) you study.
  • Pooling is wrong by large factors. Pooling the 120 events gives each window the weight 1/3. The true weights are \(\sigma_k / \sum\sigma\): about 0.99, 0.013 and 0.001. Pooling therefore overweights the upper windows by factors of about 25 and 400. The pooled spectrum is too high everywhere: by a factor of 2–3 at a few GeV, and by a factor of 100 or more above 8 GeV (less only in the bin of the spike). Its shape says more about our choice of windows than about physics.
  • The sum is the spectrum of hard scatterings with p̂T > 10 GeV. Scatterings below 10 GeV were not generated. They would add to the hadron spectrum at low \(p_T\), so below several GeV the sum is incomplete. Choose the lowest window's edge low enough for the \(p_T\) range you study.

And the bulk? For bulk observables, each window is the same backgrounds with a different jet on top. The jet's own share is small, so the windows differ little, and the weighted sum is practically the lowest window. Per window, at \(|\eta| < 1\):

What to notice.

  • Each job's estimate is uncertain by about 20–25 %, and the four scatter by about that much. Combined, the error is about 12 % per window. The jobs agree with each other within their errors (a \(\chi^2\) between 1 and 3 for 3 degrees of freedom), so the quoted errors are realistic.
  • This error is a normalisation. It moves a whole window up or down, the same for every \(p_T\) bin. It does not shrink with more oversamples, only with more tried events.
  • It does not depend on the medium. The hard scattering is the same PYTHIA process in Au+Au as in p+p. So the cross sections can come from a separate, cheap PYTHIA run with many events per window. The p+p reference pp_ref has 1,500 events per window (500 per job); tutorial 08 uses its cross sections, which are known to about 2 %.

How much does the 12 % matter for the combined spectrum? Compare it with the statistical errors, window by window. Two statistical errors, as in section 2: the reader's sampling error, and the spread of the 40 events of each window (different jets have very different fragments):

docs.title: 05 · Hadrons: spectra, dN/dη, oversamples and weights¶
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes · Needs: any setup · Data: auau_stats: the hadron files (0.2 GB, downloaded once)

A campaign of jet events is many files, many events, and for each event many samples of its hadrons. Reading them is easy. Combining them correctly takes some care: which average is the right one, how a background shared by several events counts, and how events from different p̂T windows are put together. This tutorial reads a small campaign of 120 central Au+Au events and:

  • explains what a unit, a sample and an oversample are, and why each event is the mean over its oversamples;
  • measures the charged-hadron \(dN/d\eta\) and the identified spectra of π, K and p, for the background and for the jet events;
  • combines three p̂T windows with their cross sections, and shows what goes wrong without them;
  • looks at how well a window's cross section is known;
  • checks the campaign for bad runs.

Reference pages: Hadrons, What a production writes.

Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics. The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

The outputs shown were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal.

docs.title: 1. The campaign¶
docs.text:
The set auau_stats holds four production jobs of 30 events each. Every job made 5 central (0–10 %) Au+Au backgrounds at \(\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200\) GeV and, on each background, 6 jets: 2 in each of the p̂T windows 10–20, 20–30 and 30–50 GeV. p̂T is the transverse momentum of the hard scattering in its centre-of-mass frame. The leading hard parton was required to have rapidity \(|y| < 0.6\).

These are hadrons-only jobs (run_prod_jet.py --hadrons-only): the hadrons were sampled inside the job, and no pair or particlize file was kept. The event record (background, p̂T window, deposited energy, ...) is then stored in the hadron files themselves (units/), and HadronFileReader reads it from there. It needs the files on disk, so we download them once:

docs.title: 2. Units, samples and oversamples¶
docs.text:
Units. Every hadron has a PDG id pid, a status, and a four-momentum p = \((E, p_x, p_y, p_z)\) in GeV. These files have no positions (--no-x): x is empty. The reader adds the derived columns pt, eta (pseudorapidity), y (rapidity), phi and charged.

Oversamples. The fluid ends on a freeze-out surface, where it turns into hadrons. The Cooper–Frye formula gives the mean number of each hadron species emitted from each piece of the surface. One random draw of hadrons from it is one oversample. Drawing many oversamples from the same surface beats down the noise of the sampling. But they all come from the same fluid, the same initial state and the same jet: ten oversamples are not ten collisions. Likewise, the ten fragmentations of jet_frag are ten hadronizations of the same final partons.

Look at event 0 (and the background it sits on):

docs.title: 3. Charged-hadron \(dN/d\eta\)¶
docs.text:
The number of charged hadrons per unit of pseudorapidity is the first thing measured in a heavy-ion collision. We take it for the background, and for the jet events (bulk_jet + jet_frag). Both are per event: each event is the mean over its oversamples.

The reader returns values and errors. We put them into hist histograms with Weight storage, which carry both and draw with error bars:

docs.title: 4. Identified spectra at midrapidity¶
docs.text: Now the transverse-momentum spectra of pions, kaons and protons at \(|y| < 0.5\), per event and per unit of rapidity, summed over both charges. A callable mask selects species and rapidity; it does not depend on the event, so per_event=False lets the reader bin each background only once:

docs.title: 5. The event record, and checks for bad runs¶
docs.text: Each event's record (its p̂T, its background, the energy the jet gave to the fluid, ...) is in the units/ group of the jet files. One table for the whole campaign:

docs.title: 6. p̂T windows and their cross sections¶
docs.text: PYTHIA generates hard scatterings with a steeply falling p̂T distribution. To get events at large p̂T without generating millions at low p̂T, the production splits p̂T into windows and generates the same number of events in each. Each window \(k\) then stands for a different probability: its cross section \(\sigma_k\), which PYTHIA estimates while it generates the window. The production records it per job:

docs.title: 7. How well is a window's cross section known?¶
docs.text:
PYTHIA estimates \(\sigma_k\) by Monte Carlo integration, from the events it generated in that window. These jobs generated very few: 10 accepted events per window and job, after the rapidity cut threw away about half of the 14–24 tried. Two things limit the estimate:

  • PYTHIA's own integration error, which falls like \(1/\sqrt{N_\text{tried}}\);
  • the acceptance of the parton cut, a binomial fraction: 10 kept of 19 tried is 0.53 ± 0.11, a 22 % error. This is most of each job's error.

Each job made its own estimate. Compare the four:

docs.title: Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. Pooling with weights. Fill one histogram from all 120 events, but give each event the weight \(\sigma_k / N_k\) of its window (\(N_k\) = 40). Check that this reproduces combined. Why is it the same thing?
  2. The wake per window. In section 6 the wake per window had errors of ±2.7. How many events per window would you need to see a difference of 3 hadrons between the windows at 3 standard deviations? Compare with the correlated sampling of tutorial 07.
  3. Strange baryons. Repeat section 4 for Λ (pid 3122) and Ω (pid 3334) with a mask np.isin(np.abs(ev.pid), [3122]). How do their \(\langle p_T \rangle\) fit in the mass ordering?
  4. One background, six jets. Take the six events of background 0 (events rows 0–5). Plot their jet_frag charged-hadron \(p_T\) spectra separately. Which differ most, and why?

docs.text:

  • The same hadrons in ROOT: tutorials 09 and 10, and ROOT and C++.
  • The wake in hadrons with correlated sampling: tutorial 07 and Hydro and hadrons together.
  • Everything the reader does: Hadrons.

What to notice. The hard scattering happened in the lower part of the fireball, about 3 fm from its edge. One parton heads out (down) and leaves the medium after a few fm: its few droplets lie along its short path. The other heads in (up), crosses the whole fireball, and deposits the largest share, 22 of the 54 GeV. Where a hard scattering happens decides how much medium each parton crosses. That path length is one of the main reasons jets in the same event lose different amounts of energy.

What to notice.

  • Early on, the wake is a hot spot around each new droplet: the fluid has had no time to move yet.
  • Later, it becomes a cone with a depletion behind it. The jet moves at the speed of light, faster than sound in the plasma (\(c_s \approx 1/\sqrt 3\)). A source moving faster than sound drives a Mach cone, a front of compressed, hotter fluid at an angle \(\cos\theta_M = c_s / v\) to its path. The fluid it pushes along leaves less behind it: the diffusion wake, the blue region along the jet's past path.
  • The expanding fireball carries and distorts the wake. The background has strong radial flow, so the wake drifts outward and does not keep the shape of a cone in a static medium.
  • The scale shrinks quickly (see the colour bars): the deposited energy spreads over more and more fluid, and the whole fireball cools as it expands.

The wake also spreads along \(\eta_s\). Summing \(\tau\,\Delta e\) over the transverse plane gives its profile in \(\eta_s\) (the local energy per unit \(\eta_s\), in the fluid's Bjorken frame):

The two hard partons are near midrapidity (\(y = -0.5\) and \(-0.2\)), so most of the wake sits around \(\eta_s \approx -0.5\). It stays narrow in \(\eta_s\): the fluid's longitudinal expansion keeps it close to where it was deposited. The small peak at \(\eta_s \approx 1.4\) comes from a soft parton at \(y = 1.4\).

eos = np.load("_common/eos_hotqcd_91.npz")            # MUSIC's EoS: e, P [GeV/fm^3]
def pressure(e):
    e = np.maximum(e, 1e-12)
    low = e * eos["P"][0] / eos["e"][0]                  # below the table: P proportional to e
    return np.where(e < eos["e"][0], low, np.interp(np.log(e), np.log(eos["e"]), eos["P"]))

ETA_WIN = 1.0
win = np.abs(eta) < ETA_WIN

def energy(fr, tau):
    """Lab energy [GeV] of the fluid in |eta_s| < ETA_WIN through the tau surface."""
    e, vx, vy, vz = (fr[c][..., win] for c in range(4))
    g2 = 1.0 / (1.0 - np.clip(vx**2 + vy**2 + vz**2, 0, 1 - 1e-12))
    p = pressure(e)
    w = (e + p) * g2
    dens = np.cosh(eta[win]) * (w - p) - np.sinh(eta[win]) * w * vz
    return tau * A["dx"] * A["dy"] * A["deta"] * dens.sum()

What to notice.

  • The fluid follows the deposits step by step. Every droplet shows up as a rise of the fluid's energy when it is deposited. At the end, the window holds two thirds to all of the energy deposited in it (67–99 %).
  • Part of the wake leaves the window. The wake spreads along \(\eta_s\) (section 3), so some of it crosses \(|\eta_s| = 1\). All droplets of events 3 and 4 lie inside the window, and the window keeps 80–90 % of them; counted over the whole grid, the fluid keeps all of it (exercise 3).
  • The stored grid is coarse for late deposits. The pair file's grid is coarser than MUSIC's own (0.39 against 0.3 fm in \(x\) and \(y\), 0.31 against 0.2 in \(\eta_s\)). Energy deposited late, as small hot spots in fluid near freeze-out, is not represented well on it. Event 0 deposits 13 GeV in the window after 6 fm/c, and its window keeps 67 %. Rerunning the same job with run_prod_jet.py --native, which stores MUSIC's own grid (the same events and droplets), the window keeps 92 %.
  • This matters for machine learning. A model trained on the stored grid, such as the FNO hydro of js-contrib, learns the late, small structures of the wake only in this smeared form. A bookkeeping like this one is a simple test of a grid before it is used for training.
  • It is a check, not an exact conservation law: the viscous part of \(T^{\mu\nu}\) is not stored, and energy flows across the window's edges.

What to notice. The delay follows the energy deposited late much more closely than the total. Event 1 deposited 34 GeV, all of it before \(\tau = 5.7\) fm/c, and its jet leg freezes out together with the background: energy deposited early, into hot fluid, spreads out and cools with the rest of the fireball. Event 3 deposited only 16 GeV, but half of it after 6 fm/c, into fluid already near \(T_\text{fo}\): a small reheated region then outlives the background by 2 fm/c. With five events this is an illustration, not a measurement.

The hadrons from the jet leg's surface carry this extra energy: that is the hadronic wake of tutorial 07.

docs.title: 06 · The hydro pair: the wake in the fluid¶
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes · Needs: any setup · Data: auau_pair_mini (streamed, ~40 MB read), derived (0.2 MB)

A jet that crosses the quark–gluon plasma loses energy to it. The plasma picks that energy up, and the fluid responds: a wake. The production computes each event twice, once without the jet and once with the energy the jet deposited. The difference of the two fluids is the wake and nothing else. This tutorial follows one jet through a central Au+Au collision:

  • where the jet deposits its energy, and when;
  • what the wake looks like and how it moves through the expanding fluid;
  • whether the fluid holds the energy the jet lost;
  • how the wake delays the freeze-out.

Reference pages: Hydro and hadrons together, and The physics, sections 4–6.

Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics. The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

The outputs shown were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal.

docs.title: 1. The pair and its grid¶
docs.text: arr and arr_bg hold, for each event, the energy density \(e\) and the flow velocity \((v_x, v_y, v_z)\) on a grid in \(x\), \(y\), the space-time rapidity \(\eta_s\) and the proper time \(\tau\). Each chunk on disk is one event at one \(\tau\), so reading a few frames fetches only those frames. We take event 0, whose jets deposited the most energy (54 GeV), and read the frames we need once.

docs.title: 2. The jet and where it deposits¶
docs.text: The shower initiators are the partons from the hard scattering (and the softer ones PYTHIA adds) that enter the medium. The droplets are what the CausalLiquefier made of the energy and momentum they lost: each droplet is a small source of \((E, \vec p)\) at a point in space-time, which the fluid absorbs after a delay of 1 fm/c.

docs.title: 3. The wake¶
docs.text: The wake is \(\Delta e = e_\text{jet} - e_\text{bg}\). Both legs started from the same initial condition, so before the first droplet arrives \(\Delta e = 0\) exactly; afterwards it is the fluid's response to the jet alone. Summed over \(|\eta_s| < 1\) and drawn at four times (red: more energy than without the jet; blue: less):

docs.title: 4. Does the fluid keep the jet's energy?¶
docs.text:
If the fluid keeps what the jet deposits, the energy of the jet leg minus that of the background should follow the energy of the droplets deposited so far. We count both at midrapidity, \(|\eta_s| < 1\), where the two hard partons are.

The energy of the fluid that crosses a surface of constant \( au\) is

\[E = \int au\, dx\, dy\, d\eta_s \left[\cosh\eta_s\, T^{00} - \sinh\eta_s\, T^{30} ight],\] with the ideal-fluid energy–momentum tensor \(T^{\mu u} = (e + P)u^\mu u^ u - P g^{\mu u}\), so \(T^{00} = (e + P)\gamma^2 - P\) and \(T^{30} = (e + P)\gamma^2 v_z\). The pressure \(P(e)\) comes from MUSIC's equation of state, a small table that ships with the tutorials (_common/eos_hotqcd_91.npz). The droplets' deposit times and positions are in the derived set (wake_observables.h5). We take every fifth frame (0.5 fm/c), which reads about a third of the pair file.

docs.title: 5. The wake delays the freeze-out¶
docs.text: The deposited energy reheats the fluid around the jet, so the jet leg needs longer to cool below \(T_\text{fo}\). Is it the total energy that matters, or when it was deposited?

docs.title: Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. The Mach angle. In the \(\tau = 8\) fm/c map, estimate the opening angle of the front relative to the jet's direction. Compare it with \(\cos\theta_M = c_s\) for \(c_s^2 = 1/3\), and think about why the expanding, flowing background changes it.
  2. Another event. Set EVENT = 3 (16 GeV deposited, the smallest) and rerun the notebook. How do the wake's size and the freeze-out delay compare with event 0?
  3. The window. Set ETA_WIN = 2, then ETA_WIN = 5 (the whole stored grid), and rerun section 4. How do the ratios of events 3 and 4 change? What does that say about where their wake goes?
  4. The flow of the wake. The velocity is in channels 1–3. Plot the momentum density of the wake, \(\Delta(e\,\vec v_\perp)\) (approximately), as arrows (plt.quiver) on the \(\tau = 5\) fm/c map. Which way does the fluid in the depletion move?

difference: 8.38 +- 0.67 (paired)   vs   +- 4.07 (legs treated as independent)

Correlated sampling. Each sample of a leg is one Cooper–Frye sampling of its surface: about 1,400 charged hadrons with Poisson-like fluctuations of ±40. Sampled independently, those fluctuations would bury a difference of 8 hadrons. These files were made with hadronize.py --correlated: sample \(k\) of the jet leg and sample \(k\) of its background draw the same random numbers cell by cell, so where the two surfaces agree (almost everywhere) they produce the same hadrons. The noise cancels in the difference, but only when it is taken sample by sample (paired, chosen automatically for correlated files). Treating the legs as independent overestimates the error several times over.

def lead_phi(info):
    """Azimuth of the event's hardest shower initiator."""
    ini = info.initiators()                         # shower, pid, pstat, px, py, pz, E, ...
    k = np.argmax(np.hypot(ini[:, 3], ini[:, 4]))
    return np.arctan2(ini[k, 4], ini[k, 3])

What to notice.

  • The wake sits around both jets. It has a peak near \(\Delta\phi = 0\) and another near \(\pi\), each broader than the jet's own fragments. The fluid carries the deposited energy along the jet's direction and spreads it in angle (the Mach-cone front of tutorial 06).
  • The wake is a sizable part of the soft hadrons of the jet event. Below 4 GeV it adds to the fragments over a wide range of angles. A measured jet with a large radius therefore contains medium response, and a jet with a small radius loses part of it.
  • No significant depletion is visible here. The diffusion wake of tutorial 06 is a deficit of energy density behind the jet. In hadrons it is spread over a large region and is small compared with the excess. Finding it takes many more events (and is an active topic of measurements).

What to notice.

  • The wake is harder than the bulk: its mean \(p_T\) is about 0.8 GeV against 0.57 GeV. Its hadrons come from fluid the jet heated and pushed, which moves faster toward the surface than the surrounding medium. The flow blue-shifts their spectrum.
  • Its chemistry is the bulk's. The K/π and p/π ratios of the wake agree with the background's within errors: the wake freezes out at the same temperature, so it produces hadron species in the same thermal proportions. Only the flow (the \(p_T\)) differs.

These are 5 events from one background. The campaign analysis (analysis/wake_hadrons.py, on 285 events) found the same: a wake with thermal chemistry, a harder spectrum, and energy balance within errors.

docs.title: 07 · The hadron pair: the wake in hadrons¶
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes · Needs: any setup · Data: auau_pair_mini: the hadron and particlize files (0.8 GB, downloaded once)

Tutorial 06 found the jet's wake in the fluid. Experiments see hadrons, so the question is whether the wake survives the step from fluid to hadrons, and what it looks like there.

The production samples hadrons from both freeze-out surfaces: bulk_jet from the jet leg and bulk_bg from the background. Their difference is the wake in hadrons, and adding jet_frag (the jet's own hadrons) gives the whole jet event. This tutorial:

  • measures that difference with HadronFileReader and correlated sampling;
  • shows the wake's shape around the jet;
  • checks its energy against the fluid's;
  • compares its spectrum and chemistry with the bulk's.

Reference pages: Hydro and hadrons together, Hadrons.

Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics. The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

The outputs shown were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal.

docs.title: 1. The files, and the reader¶
docs.text: HadronFileReader reads a campaign's hadron files together with their particlize files, which hold each event's record: its background, its p̂T window, its shower initiators. It reads files on disk, so we download what it needs once (about 0.8 GB). The 0.8 GB hydro pair file is not needed here.

docs.title: 2. A small difference of two large numbers¶
docs.text: At midrapidity (\(|\eta| < 1\)), a central Au+Au collision makes about 1,400 charged hadrons. The jet deposited a few tens of GeV, which should add a handful. Here are the two legs and their difference, averaged over events. For each event, its jet leg's samples are averaged and its own background's samples subtracted:

docs.title: 3. The wake around the jet¶
docs.text:
Now the shape. We take the azimuth of each hadron relative to the event's hardest shower initiator, \(\Delta\phi\), for soft charged hadrons (\(0.2 < p_T < 4\) GeV, \(|\eta| < 1\)). The two jets of a dijet are back to back, so one sits at \(\Delta\phi = 0\) and the other near \(\pi\).

The reader returns values and errors. We put them into hist histograms with Weight storage, which carry both and draw with error bars:

docs.title: 4. The wake's energy in hadrons¶
docs.text: Per event, the energy of all wake hadrons (all \(\eta\), all species), next to the energy the jet deposited in the fluid:

docs.title: 5. The wake's spectrum and chemistry¶
docs.text: Is the wake just "more of the same bulk", or different? Its \(p_T\) spectrum, normalised to one hadron, against the background's:

docs.title: Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. The wake per event. Pass events=[g] to jet_minus_background and redraw the \(\Delta\phi\) wake for event 0 and event 1 separately. Which of the two jets made the larger wake? Compare with the droplet energies of tutorial 06.
  2. The wake in \(\Delta\eta\). Replace \(\Delta\phi\) by \(\Delta\eta\) to the leading parton (its pseudorapidity is np.arcsinh(pz / pT) of the initiator). How far in \(\eta\) does the wake reach?
  3. Inside a jet cone. Count the wake's charged hadrons within \(\Delta R < 0.4\) of the leading parton, and within \(\Delta R < 1.5\). What fraction of the wake would a jet of radius 0.4 contain?
  4. Independent sampling. How many events would you need for the same error on the midrapidity difference without correlated sampling? (Use e_indep and e_paired.)
